chapters.title: Dedication
paragraphs: You draw near once more, you wavering forms — figures that long ago appeared to my dim sight. Will I try this time to hold you fast? Does my heart still incline toward that old illusion? You crowd in upon me — well then, take possession, rise around me out of vapor and mist; my breast feels stirred with youthful tremor by the magic breath that hangs about your train.

You bring with you the images of happier days, and many a beloved shadow rises with them; like an old, half-forgotten tale, first love and friendship come up alongside; the pain is renewed, and the lament repeats life's labyrinthine, wandering course, naming the good ones who, deceived by fortune of their fair hours, have vanished from my sight.

They cannot hear the songs that follow now — the souls to whom I sang the first ones. The friendly throng has scattered, the first echo has died away. My song now sounds to a strange crowd, and even their applause makes my heart anxious; and whoever once took joy in my songs, if they still live, wanders scattered through the world.

And a long-disused longing seizes me for that quiet, solemn realm of spirits. My murmuring song now hovers in uncertain tones, like an Aeolian harp; a tremor takes hold of me, tear follows tear, the stern heart feels itself grown mild and soft. What I possess I see as if at a great distance, and what has vanished becomes real to me again.

chapters.title: Prelude on the Stage
paragraphs: DIRECTOR. You two, who have so often stood by me in trouble and distress — tell me, what do you hope our undertaking will achieve here in German lands? I dearly want to please the crowd, especially since they live and let me live. The posts are set, the boards laid down, and everyone expects a festival. They sit there with eyebrows raised, expecting astonishment, ready to be dazzled. I know how to speak to the public's mood — but never have I been in such a fix as today. They aren't accustomed to the best, but they have read a fearful lot. How do we get them something fresh, with substance, and pleasing too? I won't deny I love to see the crowd flow toward our booth, surging in waves through the narrow gate of grace, fighting to push through to the ticket window in broad daylight, before four o'clock — almost coming to blows for it, like starving men at a baker's door for bread. This miracle, on so many people, only the poet performs. My friend, do it today!

POET. Oh, don't speak to me of that motley mass — at the sight of it, my spirit takes flight. Hide from me the heaving press that drags us against our will into the whirlpool. No, lead me into the quiet, narrow heaven where pure joy alone blooms for the poet, where love and friendship, with the hand of the gods, create and nourish the blessing of our heart.

Ah! What sprang up in our deepest breast, what the lips have shyly stammered out — botched now, perhaps succeeding now — the violence of the wild moment devours. Often only after years of struggle does it appear in finished form. What glitters is born for the moment; what is genuine remains unlost to posterity.

MERRY-ANDREW. If only I didn't have to hear about posterity. Suppose I wanted to talk about posterity — who then would entertain the present age? It wants its fun, and it should have it. The presence of a fine fellow is, I'd say, already something. Whoever knows how to share himself comfortably will not be soured by the people's mood; he wants a wide circle around him, so that he may move it the more surely. Be a good model, then; show what fancy is, with all its choruses — sense, reason, feeling, passion. But mind you — no lack of foolery!

DIRECTOR. But above all, let plenty happen! People come to look — they want most of all to see. If a great deal is spun out before their eyes, so that the crowd can gawk in astonishment, you have already won them over by sheer breadth, and you'll be a much-loved man. Only by mass can you sway the masses; everyone in the end picks out something for himself. Whoever brings a lot brings something to many, and each one goes home satisfied. Give us a piece — give it to us in pieces! Such a stew is bound to succeed: it's easy to set out, easy to think up. What good does it do you to deliver a finished whole? The public will pick it apart anyway.
POET. You don't feel how shabby such a craft is — how little it suits the true artist! The bungling of these tidy gentlemen is, I see, already a maxim among you.

DIRECTOR. Such a reproach leaves me unwounded. A man who plans to work effectively must keep to the best tools. Bear in mind, you have soft wood to split, and look at whom you are writing for! If boredom drives one of them, another comes stuffed from an over-loaded meal — and worst of all, many come straight from reading the newspaper. They come to us absent-minded, as one goes to a masquerade, with curiosity alone giving them wings. The ladies put themselves and their finery on display, performing without pay. What are you dreaming of up on your poetic heights? What makes a full house glad? Look closely at your patrons! Half of them are cold, half are coarse. After the play one wants a card game, another a wild night in the arms of a whore. Why, you poor fools, why bother the gracious Muses for this purpose? I tell you, just give them more, more, always more — that way you will never miss the mark. Try only to confuse the people; it's hard to satisfy them. — What's gotten into you? Rapture or pain?

POET. Go and find yourself another servant! Should the poet then frivolously throw away — for your sake — the highest right, the human right that nature granted him? By what does he move every heart? By what does he conquer every element? Is it not the harmony that wells up out of the breast and winds the world back into the heart? When nature, indifferent, spins the endless thread of length onto the spindle, when the clashing throng of all beings sounds out of tune in unwilling discord — who divides the flowing, ever-uniform line, animating it so that it moves rhythmically? Who calls the single phenomenon to consecration in the universal chorus, where it strikes the magnificent chord? Who lets the storm rage with passion? The sunset glow burn in solemn meaning? Who scatters all the lovely blossoms of spring on the path of the beloved? Who weaves the green, unimportant leaves into a wreath of honor for every kind of merit? Who secures Olympus, who gathers the gods? It is the power of man, revealed in the poet.

MERRY-ANDREW. Then use these fine powers, and run the poet's business the way one runs a love affair. By chance one approaches, one feels, one stays, and little by little one gets entangled. Happiness grows, then it is troubled. Rapture comes, then anguish, and before you know it, there it is — a romance. Let us give them just such a play! Reach into the full human life! Everyone lives it, but few know it; and wherever you grab it, it's interesting. In motley pictures, little clarity, much error, and a spark of truth — that's how the best brew is mixed, refreshing and edifying for everyone. The bloom of youth gathers around your work and drinks the revelation; every tender soul draws melancholy nourishment from your show; one thing or another is stirred up in each of them, each one sees what he carries in his heart. They are still ready alike to weep and to laugh; they still revere flight, take pleasure in appearance. The man who is finished is never to be pleased; the one who is still becoming will always be grateful.

POET. Then give me back those days when I was still becoming, when an unbroken spring of crowded songs welled up new and new again — when fog veiled the world for me, when the bud still promised wonders, when I plucked the thousand flowers that filled every valley. I had nothing, and yet enough — the urge toward truth and joy in illusion. Give me back those unbroken drives, the deep, painful happiness, the force of hate, the power of love. Give me back my youth.

MERRY-ANDREW. Youth, my good friend, you may need at most when enemies press you in battle, when the loveliest girls hang round your neck by force, when far ahead the wreath beckons from the swift race's hard-reached goal, when, after the wild whirling dance, you feast and drink the night away. But to strike the familiar lyre with grace and courage, to sweep with sweet aimlessness toward a self-set goal — that, gentlemen of advancing age, is your duty. And we don't honor you any less for it. Age does not make us childish, as people say. It only finds us still the true children.

DIRECTOR. Words enough have been exchanged. Let me see deeds at last. While you spin compliments, something useful could get done. What good is talk of mood? It never visits the man who hesitates. Once you give yourselves out as poets, then command poetry. You know what we want — we want strong drink. Brew it for me without delay! What today is not done, tomorrow stays undone. Don't lose a single day. Resolution lays hold of the possible promptly by the hair, won't let it go, and works on, because it has to.

You know on our German stages each man tries whatever he likes. So today don't spare me painted backdrops, nor the machinery. Use the great heavenly light and the small one; you may squander the stars. Of water, fire, rocky walls, of beasts and birds, there is no shortage. So in the narrow boards of the booth, stride through the whole circle of creation — and walk, with deliberate haste, from heaven through the world down to hell.

chapters.title: Prologue in Heaven
paragraphs: RAPHAEL. The sun resounds, in the old way, through brother-spheres in choral contest, and completes its prescribed journey with the stride of thunder. The sight of it gives strength to the angels, though none of them can fathom it. The unfathomably high works are as glorious as on the first day.

GABRIEL. And swift, inconceivably swift, the splendor of the earth turns round; paradisal brightness alternates with deep, shuddering night. The sea foams up in broad streams against the deep base of the rocks, and rock and sea are torn along together in the eternal swift course of the spheres.

MICHAEL. And storms rage as if in contest from sea to land, from land to sea, and form, in their rage, a chain of deepest effect all around. There a lightning devastation flames before the path of the thunderclap. But your messengers, Lord, revere the gentle wandering of your day.
ALL THREE. The sight gives the angels strength, since none can fathom you, and all your high works are as glorious as on the first day.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Since you, O Lord, are once again drawing near and asking how everything stands with us, and since you used to like seeing me about — well, here I am too among the household. Forgive me, I can't make grand speeches, even if the whole circle mocks me; my pathos would surely make you laugh, if you hadn't given up laughing. Of suns and worlds I have nothing to say. I only see how human beings torment themselves. The little god of the world is always cut from the same cloth, and is just as odd as on the first day. He'd live a little better if you hadn't given him that gleam of heavenly light. He calls it reason and uses it for one purpose only — to be more bestial than any beast. He seems to me, by Your Grace's leave, like one of those long-legged grasshoppers that always flies, and flying leaps, and right back in the grass sings its same old little song. And if only he'd stay there in the grass! He has to stick his nose into every kind of muck.
THE LORD. Have you nothing else to tell me? Have you only ever come to accuse? Is nothing on earth ever right for you?
MEPHISTOPHELES. No, Lord — I find it down there, as always, thoroughly bad. Human beings move me to pity in their days of misery; I can't even bring myself to torment the poor wretches.
THE LORD. Do you know Faust?
MEPHISTOPHELES. The doctor?
THE LORD. My servant!

MEPHISTOPHELES. Indeed! He serves you in his own peculiar way. The fool's drink and food are not earthly. The ferment in him drives him into the distance — he's half conscious of his own madness. From heaven he demands the loveliest stars, from earth every highest pleasure, and no nearness and no distance can satisfy that deeply stirred breast.

THE LORD. Even if he serves me only confusedly now, I will soon lead him into clarity. The gardener, after all, knows that when the little tree turns green, blossom and fruit will adorn the years to come.
MEPHISTOPHELES. What will you bet? You'll yet lose him to me — if you'll only give me leave to lead him, gently, down my road.
THE LORD. As long as he lives on earth, that long it shall not be forbidden to you. Man errs as long as he strives.
MEPHISTOPHELES. I thank you for that — for I've never cared to bother with the dead. What I love best are full, fresh cheeks. For a corpse I'm not at home; with me it's like the cat with the mouse.

THE LORD. Very well, it is left to you! Draw this spirit away from his original source, and lead him, if you can hold him, downward along your way — and stand ashamed when you must confess: a good man, in his dark striving, is well aware of the right path.

MEPHISTOPHELES. All right then! Only it won't take long. I'm not in the least worried about my wager. If I reach my goal, you must allow me a triumph from the depths of my breast. Dust shall he eat, and with relish — like my cousin, the famous Snake.

THE LORD. There too you may appear freely; I have never hated your kind. Of all the spirits who deny, the rogue is the least burdensome to me. Man's activity can all too easily slacken; he soon comes to love unconditional rest. So I gladly give him the companion who provokes and works on him — and who, as devil, must create. But you, the true sons of God, take joy in the living, rich beauty! Let what is becoming, what eternally works and lives, embrace you with love's gentle limits — and what hovers in wavering appearance, fix it with enduring thoughts.
[Heaven closes; the archangels disperse.]
MEPHISTOPHELES alone. From time to time I like seeing the old fellow, and I take care not to break with him. It's quite handsome of so great a Lord to speak so humanly with the Devil himself.
Of the Tragedy
Part One.

chapters.title: Night
paragraphs: FAUST. Now I have studied — alas! — philosophy, jurisprudence and medicine, and unfortunately theology too, all of it through and through, with hot striving. And here I stand now, poor fool that I am, no wiser than before. They call me Master, even Doctor, and for nearly ten years now I have led my pupils by the nose — up, down, sideways and crooked — and I see that we can know nothing! It almost burns my heart out. True, I am cleverer than all those fops — doctors, masters, scribes, and priests; no scruples or doubts torment me, I fear neither hell nor devil. But for that, all joy has been wrenched from me. I don't fool myself that I know anything worth knowing, don't fool myself that I could teach anything that might better or convert mankind. I have neither goods nor money, nor honor and worldly glory. No dog would want to live like this any longer! That is why I have given myself to magic — hoping that through the power and mouth of the spirit, some secrets might be made known to me. So that I no longer have to say, with bitter sweat, what I do not know; so that I may grasp what holds the world together at its innermost core, behold every working force and seed, and rummage no longer in mere words.

Oh, if you, full moonlight, would look on my pain for the last time — you, before whom I have so often kept midnight watch at this desk, where then, over books and paper, you would appear to me, my melancholy friend! Ah, if I could walk on mountain heights in your dear light, hover with spirits round mountain caves, weave among meadows in your half-light, freed of all the fumes of knowledge, bathed healthy in your dew!

Alas! Am I still stuck in this dungeon? Cursed, dank hole in a wall! Where even the dear light of heaven breaks dimly through painted panes. Hemmed in by this heap of books that worms gnaw and dust covers, where, all the way up to the high vault, smoke-stained paper is stuck in everywhere; surrounded by glasses, jars, instruments crammed in, ancestors' household junk piled on top — that is your world! That is what you call a world!

And do you still ask why your heart pounds anxiously in your breast? Why an unexplained pain blocks every stirring of life in you? Instead of the living nature into which God set human beings, only an animal skeleton and dead bones surround you in smoke and mold.

Flee! Up! Out into the open country! And this mysterious book, in Nostradamus' own hand — is it not escort enough for you? You will then know the courses of the stars, and when nature instructs you, the soul's power will rise in you, as one spirit speaks to another. In vain that dry brooding tries to explain these holy signs to you. You spirits, you hover beside me — answer me, if you hear me!
[He opens the book and sees the sign of the Macrocosm.]

Ha! What rapture flows in this look, all at once, through every one of my senses! I feel a young, holy joy of life rushing newly aglow through my nerves and veins. Was it a god who wrote these signs? — that still the inner raging in me, fill the poor heart with joy, and with a mysterious drive uncover the powers of nature all around me. Am I a god? Light is breaking in me. In these pure traces I see working nature lying open before my soul. Now at last I understand what the wise man says: "The world of spirits is not closed; your mind is closed, your heart is dead! Up, student, undaunted — bathe your earthly breast in the morning red!"
[He contemplates the sign.]

How everything weaves itself into a whole, each thing working and living in the other! How the powers of heaven ascend and descend and pass the golden buckets one to another! With wings that breathe of blessing, they press from heaven through the earth, sounding harmoniously through all of creation!

What a spectacle! But — alas — only a spectacle! Where shall I grasp you, infinite Nature? You breasts, where? You springs of all life, on which heaven and earth depend, toward which the withered breast strains — you flow, you give drink, and I languish here in vain?
[He turns the page in irritation and sees the sign of the Earth Spirit.]

How differently this sign works on me! You, Earth Spirit, are nearer to me. Already I feel my powers higher, already I glow as if with new wine. I feel the courage to risk myself in the world, to bear earth's woe and earth's joy, to grapple with storms, and not to flinch in the wreck's grinding. Clouds gather over me — the moon hides its light — the lamp dwindles! It smokes! Red beams flicker around my head — a shudder breathes down from the vault and seizes me! I feel it — you hover around me, spirit I have implored. Reveal yourself! Ha! How it tears at my heart! All my senses rouse to new sensations! I feel my whole heart given over to you! You must! You must! And though it cost me my life!
[He grasps the book and pronounces the sign of the Spirit mysteriously. A reddish flame flashes; the Spirit appears in the flame.]
SPIRIT. Who is calling me?
FAUST [turning aside]. Terrible vision!
SPIRIT. You have drawn me powerfully, sucked long at my sphere, and now —
FAUST. Woe! I cannot bear you!

SPIRIT. You begged, breathless, to behold me, to hear my voice, to see my face. Your soul's mighty pleading bends me — here I am! What pitiful horror grips you, you Superman! Where is the soul's call? Where is the breast that created a world within itself, and bore and nurtured it; that in tremulous joy swelled to lift itself level with us, the spirits? Where are you, Faust? — whose voice rang out to me, who pressed in on me with all his powers? Are you the one who, breathed on by my breath, trembles in all the depths of life — a fearful, recoiling worm?
FAUST. Should I yield to you, you formed-of-flame? I am he, am Faust, am your equal!

SPIRIT. In life's floods, in the storm of action, I surge up and down, weave back and forth! Birth and grave, an eternal sea, an alternating weaving, a glowing life — so I work at the whirring loom of time, and weave the living garment of God.
FAUST. You who roam the wide world, busy spirit — how near I feel to you!
SPIRIT. You resemble the spirit you can grasp — not me!
[Vanishes.]
FAUST [collapsing]. Not you! Whom, then? I, image of the Godhead! And not even your equal!
[A knock.]
Oh death! I know it — that's my assistant — my finest happiness comes to nothing. That this fullness of visions has to be disrupted by that dry creeper!
[WAGNER, in a dressing gown and nightcap, a lamp in his hand. FAUST turns away in irritation.]

WAGNER. Forgive me! I heard you declaiming. You were certainly reading a Greek tragedy? In this art I would like to learn something, for these days it has great effect. I have often heard it praised that an actor could give a parson lessons.
FAUST. Yes, when the parson is an actor — as can sometimes be the case.
WAGNER. Ah, when one is shut up in one's study like this and barely sees the world even on a holiday — barely through a telescope, only from a distance — how is one to lead it by persuasion?

FAUST. If you don't feel it, you'll never hunt it down — if it doesn't surge up out of the soul and compel the hearts of all your hearers with primal, satisfying force. Just sit there and paste things together, brew up a ragout from someone else's feast, blow up the meager flames out of your little heap of ashes! You'll get admiration from children and apes, if your palate craves it. But you will never bring heart to heart, if it doesn't come from the heart.
WAGNER. Yet delivery is what makes the orator's success; I feel that well, I am still far behind.

FAUST. Seek the honest gain! Don't be a bell-loud fool! Understanding and right sense make their own case with little art; and if you are in earnest about saying something, is it necessary to chase after words? Yes, your speeches, so glittering, in which you twist humanity's confetti into curls, are as cheerless as the misty wind that whispers through dry autumn leaves!

WAGNER. Ah God, art is long, and our life is short. With my critical striving, I often feel anxious in head and breast. How hard it is to acquire the means by which one climbs to the sources! And before one even reaches the halfway mark, a poor devil has to die.
FAUST. Parchment — is that the holy spring from which one draught quenches thirst forever? You won't have gained refreshment unless it wells up from your own soul.
WAGNER. Forgive me! It is a great delight to put oneself into the spirit of past times — to see how a wise man before us thought, and how splendidly far we have come at last.

FAUST. Oh yes, all the way to the stars! My friend, the times of the past are for us a book sealed with seven seals. What you call the spirit of the times is, at bottom, the gentlemen's own spirit, in which the times are mirrored. Then it's truly often a sorry sight! At the first glance one runs from you. A garbage bin and a junk room — and at best some grand affair of state, with splendid pragmatic maxims, the kind that suit puppets' mouths well!
WAGNER. But the world! The heart and mind of man! Surely everyone would like to know something of it.

FAUST. Yes — what people call knowing! Who dares to call the child by its right name? The few who knew anything of it — who, foolish enough not to keep their full hearts to themselves, revealed their feeling and their vision to the rabble — have always been crucified and burned. I beg you, friend, it's deep in the night; we must break off this time.

WAGNER. I would gladly have stayed up forever, to converse so learnedly with you. But tomorrow, on the first day of Easter, allow me one or two more questions. With diligence I have devoted myself to study; though I know much, I should like to know everything.
[Exit.]
FAUST [alone]. How is it that hope never fails the head that constantly clings to stale stuff, that digs with greedy hand for treasures, and is happy when it finds earthworms!

Should such a human voice sound out here, where the fullness of spirits had surrounded me? Yet — ah — for once I thank you, you most wretched of all earth's sons. You tore me free of the despair that was already trying to destroy my senses. Ah! the apparition was so giant-huge that I had to feel myself a true dwarf.

I, image of the Godhead, who already imagined myself quite close to the mirror of eternal truth, enjoyed myself in heavenly splendor and clarity, and stripped off the son of earth — I, more than cherub, whose free power already presumed, full of premonition, to flow through nature's veins and, creating, to enjoy the gods' life — how I must atone for it! A thunder-word has swept me away.

I dare not presume to be your equal. If I had the power to draw you to me, I had no power to hold you. In that blessed moment I felt myself so small, so great — and you cruelly thrust me back into the uncertain human lot. Who will teach me? What should I avoid? Should I obey that drive? Ah! Even our deeds, like our sufferings, hinder the course of our life.

Always more and more foreign matter pushes itself onto the most magnificent thing the spirit has received. When we attain the goods of this world, then the better is called illusion and delusion. The glorious feelings that gave us life freeze in earthly turmoil.

If imagination once spread out, in bold flight and full of hope, toward the eternal, now a small space is enough for it, when happiness after happiness is wrecked in the whirlpool of time. Care nests at once in the deep heart; there it works secret pains, rocks itself restlessly and disturbs pleasure and rest. It always covers itself with new masks: it can appear as house and home, as wife and child, as fire, water, dagger, poison; you tremble at everything that doesn't strike, and what you never lose, that you must always weep over.

I am not the equal of the gods! I feel that too deeply. I am the equal of the worm that burrows through the dust — that, as it lives feeding in the dust, is destroyed and buried by the wanderer's tread.

Is it not dust — that which narrows me in here, this towering wall of a hundred shelves; the trash that crowds in on me with thousandfold bric-à-brac in this moth-eaten world? Here am I supposed to find what I lack? Am I supposed to read in a thousand books that everywhere people have tormented themselves, that here and there some fortunate one has lived? — Why do you grin at me, you hollow skull? Except to say that your brain, like mine, once confused, sought the easy day and, in the heavy twilight, with the lust for truth, miserably erred. You instruments, of course, mock me with wheel and cogs, cylinder and lever. I stood at the gate; you should have been the keys. Your wards are wreathed all right, but you don't lift the bolts. Mysterious in broad daylight, nature will not let her veil be torn off, and what she will not reveal to your spirit, you will not extort from her by levers and screws. You old gear that I never used — you stand here only because my father used you. You old scroll, you have been smoked dark as long as the dim lamp has fumed at this desk. Far better had I squandered the little I had, instead of sweating here under the burden of that little! What you have inherited from your fathers, earn it in order to possess it. What is not used is a heavy load; only what the moment creates can the moment use.

But why does my gaze cling to that spot? Is that little flask there a magnet to the eyes? Why does it grow lovely-bright to me all at once? — as when in the night-wood the moon's gleam plays around us.

I greet you, you unique vial! That I now reach down with reverence — in you I revere human ingenuity and art. You essence of the gentle drowsing juices, you extract of all deadly fine powers — show your master your favor! I see you, the pain is eased; I grasp you, striving lessens; the spirit's flood-stream ebbs little by little. I am directed out into the high sea — the mirror-flood gleams at my feet; a new day lures me to new shores.

A chariot of fire hovers, on light wings, toward me! I feel ready, on a new path, to break through the ether, into new spheres of pure activity. This high life, this divine bliss! You — a worm just now — and you deserve this? Yes, turn your back resolutely on the dear earth-sun! Dare to wrench open the gates that everyone gladly slips past! Here is the time to prove by deeds that the dignity of man does not yield to the height of the gods — not to tremble before that dark cavern, in which imagination damns itself to its own torment, but to strive toward that passage, around whose narrow mouth the whole of hell flames; calmly to resolve on this step, and even at the risk of flowing on into nothingness.

Now come down, crystal pure cup! Out of your old case, which I have not thought of for many years. You glittered at our fathers' feasts, gladdened the solemn guests when one passed you to the next. The richly artful splendor of all your figures, the drinker's duty to explain them in rhyme, to empty the hollow at one draught, recalls many a night of my youth. Now I will not pass you to a neighbor; I will not show off my wit on your art. Here is a juice that quickly intoxicates. With brown flood it fills your hollow. The one I have prepared, the one I choose — let this last drink now, with the whole of my soul, be raised, as a high festal greeting, to the morning!
[He sets the cup to his lips.]
[Bell-tones and choral song.] CHORUS OF ANGELS.
Christ is risen! Joy to mortal man, whom the corrupting, creeping, hereditary failings have wound about.

FAUST. What deep humming, what bright tone, draws the glass with such force from my mouth? Are you, dull bells, already announcing the first festal hour of the Easter feast? You choirs, are you already singing the consoling song that once, around the night of the grave, sounded from angels' lips, the surety of a new covenant?
CHORUS OF WOMEN. With spices we had tended him, we his faithful had laid him out; cloths and bands we wound about him cleanly. Ah! and we find Christ no longer here.
CHORUS OF ANGELS. Christ is risen! Blessed is the loving one, who has stood the test — distressing, salutary, exercising.

FAUST. What do you seek of me, you heavenly tones, mighty and mild, here on the dust? Sound your way over there, where soft people are. I hear the message well enough, but I lack the faith. The miracle is faith's dearest child. To those spheres I do not dare to strive, from which the lovely tidings ring; and yet, accustomed to this sound from my youth, even now it calls me back into life. Once the kiss of heavenly Love would fall on me, in the solemn Sabbath stillness; how full of presentiment then was the bell's ringing, and a prayer was a fervent delight; an inconceivable lovely longing drove me through woods and meadows, and under a thousand hot tears I felt a world arising in me. This song announced the lively games of youth, the free joy of the spring festival; memory holds me back now, with childlike feeling, from the last, grave step. Oh! Sound on, you sweet songs of heaven! The tear flows — earth has me back!

CHORUS OF DISCIPLES. If the buried One has already raised himself above, the living, exalted One, gloriously risen — if he is, in joyous becoming, near to creating delight — alas, on earth's breast we are here for sorrow. He left his own pining behind here. Ah! we mourn, Master, your good fortune!

CHORUS OF ANGELS. Christ is risen, out of the womb of decay! Tear yourselves free of fetters, joyfully! You who actively praise him, who show love, who feed your brothers, who travel preaching, who promise rapture — to you the Master is near, to you he is here!

chapters.title: Before the Gate
paragraphs: FIRST GROUP. We're going out to the hunting lodge.
JOURNEYMAN. We'd rather walk over to the mill.
SECOND JOURNEYMAN. I'd advise you to go up to the Wasserhof.
SECOND GROUP. The way there isn't pretty at all.
ANOTHER. What are you doing then?
A THIRD. I'm going with the others.
A FOURTH. Come up to Burgdorf — you'll find for sure the prettiest girls there, the best beer, and brawls of the first sort.
A FIFTH. You overlively fellow — does your hide itch for a third hiding? I won't go; the place gives me chills.
SERVING-MAID. No, no! I'm going back to the city.
SECOND MAID. We'll find him standing by those poplars for sure.
FIRST MAID. That's no great luck for me. He'll walk at your side, he'll only dance with you on the green. What do your pleasures matter to me!
SECOND MAID. He's certainly not alone today; the curly-head, he says, will be with him.
STUDENT. Lord, how the bonny girls march! Brother, come on — we have to escort them. A strong beer, a sharp tobacco, and a maid in her finery — that's my taste.
TOWN GIRLS. Just look at those handsome lads! It's truly a shame — they could keep the very best company, and instead they go running after these maids!

SECOND STUDENT [to the first]. Not so fast! Two more are coming up behind. They're prettily dressed, and my neighbor is one of them — I'm very fond of that girl. They walk their quiet step, and they'll take us with them in the end after all.
FIRST STUDENT. Brother, no! I don't like to be tied down. Quick! so we don't lose our game. The hand that handles the broom on Saturday will caress you best on Sunday.

BURGHER. No, I don't like him, the new mayor! Now that he's in office, every day he gets bolder. And what does he do for the city? Doesn't it just get worse and worse? We have to obey more than ever, and pay more than ever.

BEGGAR [singing]. You good gentlemen, you fair ladies, so well-dressed and red-cheeked, deign to look at me — see and ease my misery! Don't let me grind out the tune for nothing! Only he is glad who can give. May this day, which all people celebrate, be a harvest day for me.

ANOTHER BURGHER. On Sundays and holidays I know nothing better than a chat about war and rumors of war, when far back in Turkey the peoples are striking each other down. One stands at the window, drinks one's little glass, and watches the colorful boats glide down the river. Then in the evening one goes home contented and blesses peace and peaceful times.
THIRD BURGHER. Yes, neighbor! That's how I like it too. Let them split each other's heads, let everything go to ruin — only at home let the old order stay.

OLD WOMAN [to the town girls]. Eh! How dressed up! Such pretty young blood! Who could help gawking at you? Just don't be so proud! It's all right! And what you wish for — I would know how to arrange it.
TOWN GIRL. Agatha, away! I take care not to walk in public with such witches. True, on Saint Andrew's Eve she let me see my future love in the flesh.
OTHER TOWN GIRL. She showed me mine in the crystal — soldierly, with several daring men. I look around, I search for him everywhere; only he won't appear to me.
SOLDIERS. Castles with high walls and battlements, girls with proud, scornful airs — these I would conquer! Bold is the toil, glorious the reward!

And the trumpet — we let it recruit, both for joy and for ruin. That is a storming! That is a life! Girls and castles must give themselves up. Bold is the toil, glorious the reward! And the soldiers march away.
[FAUST and WAGNER.]

FAUST. Stream and brook are freed from ice by the lovely, quickening glance of spring. In the valley, hope's joy turns green. Old Winter, in his weakness, has withdrawn into rugged mountains. From there, in flight, he sends only powerless flurries of granular ice in stripes across the greening meadow. But the sun tolerates nothing white; everywhere formation and striving stir, everything wants color of life. But there are no flowers yet in the district, so she takes dressed-up people for them. Turn around — look from these heights back at the city. Out of the hollow, gloomy gate a motley swarm presses forth. Everyone basks today so gladly. They celebrate the resurrection of the Lord, for they themselves have risen, out of the close chambers of low houses, out of the bonds of trade and craft, out of the press of gables and roofs, out of the squeezing narrowness of streets, out of the venerable night of churches, they have all been brought into the light. Look, look! How nimbly the crowd scatters through the gardens and fields, how the river, in breadth and length, sets so many merry skiffs in motion, and, loaded to the sinking point, this last boat moves off. Even from the mountain's distant paths colored clothes flash to us. I already hear the village's hubbub. Here is the people's true heaven. Great and small shout out contented: here I am human, here I may be it.

WAGNER. To walk with you, Doctor, is honorable and a benefit. But I would not lose myself out here alone, for I am an enemy of everything coarse. The fiddling, shouting, ninepin-rolling is a thoroughly hated sound to me. They rage as if driven by an evil spirit, and call it joy, call it song.
[PEASANTS UNDER THE LINDEN. Dance and Song.]

The shepherd dressed for the dance, with a colored jacket, ribbon, and wreath; he was prettily attired. Already round the linden it was crowded, and everyone was already dancing like mad. Yoo-hoo! Yoo-hoo! Yoo-hoo-ho! Heisa! Hey! That's how the fiddle-bow went.

He pressed forward in haste, and there he bumped into a girl with his elbow. The fresh wench turned around and said, "Now I find that stupid! Yoo-hoo! Yoo-hoo! Yoo-hoo-ho! Heisa! Hey! Don't be so rude."

But it went briskly round the circle. They danced right, they danced left, and all the skirts flew. They turned red, they grew warm, and rested breathless arm in arm — Yoo-hoo! Yoo-hoo! Yoo-hoo-ho! Heisa! Hey! — and hip against elbow.

"Don't be so familiar with me! How many a man has lied to and deceived his bride!" But he flattered her aside, and from the linden tree it rang out far: Yoo-hoo! Yoo-hoo! Yoo-hoo-ho! Heisa! Hey! — shouting and the fiddle-bow.

OLD PEASANT. Doctor, it is fine of you that you don't disdain us today, and walk among this throng of common folk, learned as you are. Take, then, the finest mug, which we have filled with a fresh draught. I bring it to you and wish aloud that it may not only quench your thirst — may the number of drops it holds be added to your days.
FAUST. I take the refreshing drink, and return to all of you health and thanks.
[The people gather round in a circle.] OLD PEASANT.

Truly it is very well done that you appear on this happy day, since in former times you stood by us in evil days too! Many a man stands here alive whom your father at the last tore from the raging fever, when he set a limit to the plague. You too, then a young man, went into every house of the sick. Many a corpse was carried out, but you came out hale, you stood many a hard test. The helper helped him from above.
ALL. Health to the proven man, that he may help long yet!
FAUST. Bow before the One above, who teaches helping and sends help.
[He walks on with WAGNER.]

WAGNER. What a feeling, you great man, you must have at this multitude's reverence! Oh, happy he who can draw such an advantage from his gifts! The father shows you to his boy, everyone asks and presses and hurries; the fiddle stops, the dancer waits. You go on, they stand in rows, the caps fly into the air; and they would scarcely have stopped short of bending the knee, as if the Sacrament were coming.

FAUST. Just a few more steps up to that stone — here let us rest from our wandering. Often I sat here alone, deep in thought, and tortured myself with prayer and fasting. Rich in hope, firm in faith, with tears, sighing, and wringing of hands, I thought to wrest the end of that plague from the Lord of heaven. The crowd's applause now sounds to me like mockery. Oh, if you could read inside me, you would see how little father and son were worth such fame! My father was a dark-minded honorable man, who, in honesty but in his own way, brooded with crotchety effort over nature and her sacred circles. He, in the company of adepts, shut himself in the black kitchen, and after endless recipes poured opposites together. There a Red Lion, a bold suitor, was wedded in the warm bath to the Lily, and then both were tormented with open flame from one bridal chamber to another. There then appeared, in colorful colors, the young Queen in the glass — there was the medicine; the patients died, and no one asked, who recovered? So we, with these hellish concoctions, raged in these valleys, these mountains, far worse than the plague. I myself have given the poison to thousands. They withered away — and I have to live to see people praise the brazen murderers.

WAGNER. How can you grieve over that! Doesn't an honest man do enough by exercising the art committed to him conscientiously and punctually? If, as a young man, you honor your father, you will gladly receive what he hands down; if, as a man, you increase knowledge, your son in turn can reach a higher goal.

FAUST. Oh, happy he who can still hope to surface from this sea of error! What one does not know, that is just what one needs; what one knows, one cannot use. But let us not, with such gloom, blight the lovely good of this hour! See how, in the evening sun's glow, the green-encircled cottages shimmer. The day moves on, gives way; it is outlived; over there it hurries on and quickens new life. Oh, that no wing lifts me from the ground, to strive after it and after it always! I would see, in the eternal evening beam, the still world at my feet — every height kindled, every valley calmed, the silver brook flowing into golden streams. Then no wild mountain, with all its gorges, would hinder my godlike course; already the sea, with its warmed bays, opens before astonished eyes. Yet at last the goddess seems to sink away. But the new drive awakens — I hurry on to drink her eternal light, the day before me, the night behind me, the heavens above me, and the waves below. A beautiful dream, while she escapes. Ah! to the wings of the spirit no bodily wing will so easily join. Yet it is innate in everyone — that his feeling presses upward and forward, when the lark sings her ringing song over us, lost in the blue space; when over rugged spruce-heights the eagle soars with outspread wings, and over plains, over lakes, the crane strives toward home.

WAGNER. I have often had crotchety hours myself, but such a drive I have never felt. One quickly tires of woods and fields. I will never envy the bird its wings. How differently the joys of the mind carry us, from book to book, from page to page! That makes winter nights lovely and beautiful; a blessed life warms every limb, and ah! when you unroll a worthy parchment, then the whole heaven descends to you.

FAUST. You are aware of only the one drive — oh, never come to know the other! Two souls, alas, dwell in my breast; one wants to part from the other. The one clings, in coarse love-lust, to the world with clutching organs; the other lifts itself violently from the dust, to the realms of high ancestors. Oh, if there are spirits in the air who weave, ruling, between earth and heaven, then descend from the golden mist and bear me away to a new, motley life! Yes, if only a magic mantle were mine! And carried me into foreign lands, I would not give it up for the costliest robes, not even for a king's mantle.

WAGNER. Don't summon the well-known throng, which streams and overspreads itself in the misty air, preparing thousandfold dangers for man from every side. From the north the sharp spirit-tooth presses on you, with arrow-pointed tongues; from the east they come, parching, drawing close and feeding on your lungs; if the south sends them out of the desert, piling fire upon fire about your crown, then the west brings the swarm that first refreshes only to drown you and field and meadow. They listen gladly, glad to do harm; they obey gladly, because they like to deceive us; they pose as if sent from heaven, and lisp angelically when they lie. But let us go! The world has already grown gray, the air cooled, the mist falls. Only in the evening does one truly value home. — Why do you stand like that, gazing out astonished? What can grip you so in the twilight?
FAUST. Do you see the black dog ranging through the field and stubble?
WAGNER. I saw him long ago — he didn't seem important to me.
FAUST. Look at him properly! What do you take the creature for?
WAGNER. For a poodle, who in his way is laboring to track his master.
FAUST. Do you notice, how in a wide spiral he chases around us, ever closer? And, if I am not mistaken, a streak of fire trails behind on his path.
WAGNER. I see nothing but a black poodle. With you it may well be a trick of the eyes.
FAUST. It seems to me that he is drawing magic, soft snares around our feet, for some future bond.
WAGNER. I see him springing around us uncertain and timid, because, instead of his master, he sees two strangers.
FAUST. The circle tightens — he's already close!
WAGNER. You see — it's a dog, and not a ghost. He growls and hesitates, lies down on his belly, he wags. All proper dog behavior.
FAUST. Join us! Come here!
WAGNER. He's a poodle-foolish creature. You stand still, he waits; you speak to him, he stretches up to you; lose something, he'll bring it; spring for your stick into the water.
FAUST. You're probably right — I find no trace of a spirit, and it's all training.
WAGNER. To a dog that has been well brought up, even a wise man is well disposed. Yes, your favor he wholly deserves — he, the splendid disciple of the students.
[They go in through the city gate.]

chapters.title: Study (Part I)
paragraphs: FAUST [entering with the poodle]. I have left field and meadow behind, which a deep night now covers — a night that, with prophetic, holy awe, wakes the better soul in us. Now wild urges are asleep, and every impetuous deed; the love of mankind stirs, the love of God now stirs.

Be quiet, poodle! Don't run back and forth! What are you sniffing at on the threshold? Lie down behind the stove. I'll give you my best cushion. Just as out on the mountain road you gladdened us by running and leaping, now also let me care for you, as a welcome quiet guest.

Ah, when in our narrow cell the lamp burns again, friendly, then it grows bright in our bosom, in the heart that knows itself. Reason begins to speak again, and hope begins to bloom again; we long for the streams of life — ah, for the very source of life.

Don't growl, poodle! That bestial sound doesn't suit the holy tones now embracing my whole soul. We are used to people mocking what they don't understand, growling at the good and beautiful that often inconveniences them. Will the dog also growl at it like them? But ah, even with the best will, I already feel that contentment no longer wells up out of my breast. But why must the stream so quickly run dry, and we lie thirsting again? I have so much experience of this. Yet this lack can be made up for. We learn to value the supernal; we long for revelation, which nowhere burns more worthily and beautifully than in the New Testament. I'm impelled to open the basic text, and once, with honest feeling, render the holy original into my beloved German.
[He opens a volume and sets to work.]

It is written: "In the beginning was the Word!" Already I'm stuck. Who will help me on? I cannot possibly value the word so highly. I must translate it differently, if I am truly enlightened by the spirit. It is written: in the beginning was the Sense. Consider the first line carefully — don't let your pen rush! Is it the sense that works and creates everything? It should read: in the beginning was the Power! Yet, even as I'm writing this down, something already warns me not to settle there. The spirit helps me! All at once I see the answer, and write confidently: in the beginning was the Deed!

If I am to share the room with you, poodle, then stop the howling, stop the barking! Such a disturbing companion I cannot bear in my company. One of us two must leave the cell. Reluctantly I revoke the right of hospitality — the door is open, you have free run. But what must I see! Can this happen naturally? Is it shadow, is it reality? How my poodle is growing long and broad! He rises with force — that is no shape of a dog! What a specter I have brought into the house! Already he looks like a hippopotamus, with fiery eyes, terrible jaws. Oh — I have you for sure! For such a half-hellbreed, the Key of Solomon is good.

SPIRITS [in the passage]. One inside has been caught! Stay outside, none of you follow him! Like the fox in the iron, an old hell-lynx is fretting. But pay attention! Sweep along, sweep again, up and down — and he has freed himself. If you can be of use to him, don't leave him sitting there! For he has done many a favor for all of us already.
FAUST. First, to confront the creature, I need the Charm of the Four: Salamander shall glow, Undine wind herself, Sylph vanish, Goblin labor.
Whoever did not know them — the elements, their force and properties — would be no master over the spirits.
Vanish in flames, Salamander! Rushing flow together, Undine! Shine in meteor-beauty, Sylph! Bring household help, Incubus, Incubus! Step forward and conclude.
None of the four is in this creature. He lies quite still and grins at me — I have not yet hurt him. You shall hear me conjure stronger.
Are you, fellow, a fugitive from hell? Then look at this sign! Before it the black hosts bow.
Already he swells up with bristling hair. Cast-out being! Can you read it? — Him, the never-begotten, the unutterable, poured through all heavens, brazenly pierced through.

Banished behind the stove, he swells like an elephant, fills up the whole room, wants to dissolve into mist. Don't rise to the ceiling! Lay yourself at your master's feet! You see I do not threaten in vain. I will singe you with holy flame! Don't await the thrice-glowing light! Don't await the strongest of my arts!
MEPHISTOPHELES
[steps out from behind the stove as the mist falls, dressed like a wandering scholastic]
Why all the noise? What does the gentleman require?
FAUST. So this was the poodle's core! A wandering scholastic? The case makes me laugh.
MEPHISTOPHELES. I salute the learned gentleman! You've made me sweat thoroughly.
FAUST. What is your name?
MEPHISTOPHELES. The question seems petty to me — for one who so deeply scorns the word, who, far from all appearance, strives only for the depth of being.
FAUST. With you gentlemen, one can usually read the being from the name, where it shows itself all too plainly when you're called Lord-of-Flies, Destroyer, Liar. Well — who are you, then?
MEPHISTOPHELES. A part of that power which always wills the evil and always works the good.
FAUST. What is meant by this riddling word?

MEPHISTOPHELES. I am the spirit who always denies! And rightly so; for everything that comes into being deserves to perish. Therefore it would be better that nothing should come into being. So everything that you call sin, destruction — in short, evil — is my proper element.
FAUST. You call yourself a part, and yet stand whole before me?

MEPHISTOPHELES. I speak modest truth to you. While man, that little fool's-world, usually takes himself for a whole — I am a part of the part that in the beginning was everything, a part of the darkness that gave birth to itself the light, the proud light that now disputes Mother Night's old rank, her space — and yet does not succeed, since, however much it strives, it sticks fast to bodies. From bodies it streams, it makes bodies beautiful, a body checks it on its course; so, I hope, it will not last long, and with the bodies it will perish.
FAUST. Now I know your worthy duties! You can destroy nothing on the grand scale, and so you start in on the small.

MEPHISTOPHELES. And really, not much is achieved by it. What stands against Nothingness, this Something, this clumsy world — however much I have undertaken, I haven't known how to get at it: with waves, storms, shaking, fire, in the end sea and land remain calm! And as for the damned stuff, the brood of beast and man, there's simply no harming it. How many have I already buried! And always a new fresh blood is circulating. So it goes on — one could go mad! From the air, the water, and the earth a thousand germs unfurl themselves, in dryness, wetness, warmth, cold! If I had not reserved fire for myself, I would have nothing of my own.
FAUST. So against the eternally active, the wholesomely creating power, you set the cold devil's fist that vainly clenches in malice! Try beginning something different, you strange son of Chaos!
MEPHISTOPHELES. We will really give it some thought — more on that next time! Might I take my leave for now?
FAUST. I don't see why you ask. Now I have made your acquaintance — visit me as you please. Here is the window, here the door — a chimney is certainly available to you too.
MEPHISTOPHELES. I'll just admit it — a small obstacle keeps me from walking out: the witch's foot on your threshold —
FAUST. The pentagram causes you pain? Eh, tell me, son of hell — if it bans you, how did you come in? How was such a spirit fooled?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Look at it properly! It's not well drawn. The one corner pointing outward is, as you see, a little open.
FAUST. Chance has hit on that nicely! And so you would be my prisoner? That came off by accident!
MEPHISTOPHELES. The poodle noticed nothing as he leapt in. The matter looks different now: the devil cannot get out of the house.
FAUST. But why don't you go through the window?
MEPHISTOPHELES. It's a law of devils and ghosts: where they have slipped in, there they must go out. The first is up to us; in the second we are servants.
FAUST. Hell itself has its laws? I find that good — so a pact could be made, and reliably too, with you gentlemen?

MEPHISTOPHELES. What's promised, you shall enjoy in full — none of it will be skimped from you. But it's not so quickly stated. We'll discuss it at the next opportunity. But for now I beg you, urgently, urgently, to release me this once.
FAUST. Then stay just one more moment, and first tell me good news.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Let me go now! I'll come back soon. Then you may ask whatever you please.
FAUST. I didn't lay traps for you — you walked into the snare yourself. Whoever holds the devil, let him hold him! He won't catch him so easily a second time.
MEPHISTOPHELES. If it pleases you, I'm also ready to stay here for company — but on condition that I pass the time for you with my arts, in worthy fashion.
FAUST. I'll gladly see it — that's at your discretion; only let the art be agreeable!

MEPHISTOPHELES. You will, my friend, gain more for your senses in this hour than in a year's monotony. What the delicate spirits will sing for you, the lovely images they bring, are no empty magic show. Your sense of smell will also be delighted, then your palate gratified, and then your feeling enraptured. No preparation is needed in advance — we are together, begin!

SPIRITS. Vanish, you dark vaults above! Show yourself more delightfully, the blue ether shining in! If only the dark clouds had melted away! Little stars are sparkling, milder suns shine in. The spiritual beauty of heavenly sons, in wavering bowing, hovers past. Yearning inclination follows after; and the fluttering ribbons of garments cover the lands, cover the bowers where, for life, lovers, deep in thought, give themselves up. Bower next to bower! Sprouting tendrils! Heavy bunches of grapes plunge into the vat of the pressing winepress; bubbling wines crash in streams, ripple through pure noble stones, leave the heights behind, spread out into lakes around the contentment of greening hills. And the winged things sip their bliss, fly toward the sun, fly toward the bright islands swaying playfully on the waves; where we hear chorusing rejoicers, see dancers above the meadows, who all scatter in the open. Some climb over the heights, others swim across the lakes, others soar — all toward life, all toward the distance of loving stars, blessed grace.

MEPHISTOPHELES. He's asleep! Just so, you airy, delicate boys! You have sung him faithfully into slumber! For this concert I'm in your debt. You're not yet the man to hold the devil fast! Beguile him with sweet dream-shapes, sink him into a sea of delusion. But to break the spell of this threshold I need a rat-tooth. I won't have to conjure long — already one is rustling here, and will hear me at once.

The lord of rats and mice, of flies, frogs, bedbugs, lice, commands you to come forward and gnaw at this threshold, where he is dabbing it with oil — there, you're already hopping out! Now briskly to work! The point that bound me, it sits right on the front edge. One more bite and it's done. — Now, Faust, dream on, until we meet again.
FAUST [waking]. Am I deceived once more? Does the spirit-thronged drive vanish like that — that a dream lied a devil to me, and that a poodle escaped me?

chapters.title: Study (Part II)
paragraphs: MEPHISTOPHELES. It's me. FAUST.
Come in!
MEPHISTOPHELES. You have to say it three times.
FAUST. Come in then!

MEPHISTOPHELES. So you please me. We'll get on, I hope, since to drive your dreary moods away I'm here as a noble young gentleman, in red gold-trimmed costume, the little cape of stiff silk, the cock's feather in the hat, with a long, pointed sword. I now advise you, briefly and bluntly, to put on the like — so that, untied and free, you may experience what life is.

FAUST. In any costume I will surely feel the pain of this narrow earthly life. I am too old to merely play, too young to be without desire. What can the world possibly offer me? Do without! Thou shalt do without! That is the eternal song that rings in everyone's ear, that every hour our whole life long sings hoarsely to us. Only with horror do I wake in the morning. I would weep bitter tears at seeing the day that, in its course, will not fulfill a single one of my wishes — not one — that even diminishes, with willful carping, the foretaste of every joy, that hinders the creations of my eager breast with a thousand grimaces of life. And, when night descends, I have to stretch myself anxiously upon the bed; even there no rest is granted me, wild dreams will frighten me. The god who dwells in my breast can deeply stir my innermost being; the one enthroned over all my powers — he can move nothing outward. So existence is a burden to me, death longed for, life hateful.
MEPHISTOPHELES. And yet death is never an entirely welcome guest.

FAUST. O blessed is he around whose temples death, in the gleam of victory, winds the bloody laurels — whom, after a hectic dance is danced through, he finds in a girl's arms. Oh, that I had sunk away rapt and soulless before the high spirit's power!
MEPHISTOPHELES. And yet someone, on a certain night, didn't quite drink down a brown juice.
FAUST. Spying, it seems, is your pleasure.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Omniscient I am not. But much is known to me.

FAUST. If, out of the terrible turmoil, a sweetly familiar tone drew me, deceived the remnant of childlike feeling with the echoes of a happy time — then I curse all that wraps the soul with lures and trickery, and binds it in this house of mourning by the powers of dazzlement and flattery! Cursed in advance the high opinion with which the spirit embraces itself! Cursed the dazzle of appearance that presses on our senses! Cursed what flatters us in dreams — the lies of fame and lasting name! Cursed what flatters us as possession — as wife and child, as servant and plough! Cursed be Mammon, when with treasures he stirs us to bold deeds, when for idle pleasure he arranges our cushions! A curse on the balsam-juice of grapes! A curse on that highest grace of love! Cursed be hope! Cursed faith! And, before all, cursed be patience!

CHORUS OF SPIRITS [unseen]. Woe! Woe! You have destroyed it, the beautiful world, with mighty fist; it falls, it crumbles! A demigod has shattered it! We carry the ruins over into the void, and lament over the lost beauty. Mightier of earth's sons, more splendidly build it again, build it up in your bosom! Begin a new course of life, with bright sense, and new songs will sound to it!

MEPHISTOPHELES. These are the little ones of my own. Hear how, with the wisdom of age, they advise you to pleasure and deeds! They want to lure you out into the wide world, out of the solitude where senses and sap stagnate.

Stop playing with your sorrow, which, like a vulture, feeds on your life. The worst company will let you feel that you are a man among men. Yet I don't mean to thrust you down among the rabble. I'm none of the great ones. But if you'll take your steps through life joined with me, then I'll gladly accommodate myself to be yours, on the spot. I'm your companion, and, if I do well by you, I'm your servant, your slave!
FAUST. And what shall I do for you in return?
MEPHISTOPHELES. For that you still have a long deadline.
FAUST. No, no! The devil is an egoist, and does not easily, for God's sake, do what is useful to another. Speak the condition out plainly: a servant like that brings danger into the house.
MEPHISTOPHELES. I will here bind myself in your service, never rest or pause at your beck and call; if we meet again on the other side, you shall do the same for me.

FAUST. The other side concerns me little. If you first smash this world to ruins, the other can come into being afterward. From this earth my joys spring, and this sun shines on my sorrows. Once I can part from them, then whatever wills and can may happen. I want to hear nothing further about it — whether one will hate and love in the future too, and whether in those spheres there is also an above and below.
MEPHISTOPHELES. In that frame of mind you may risk it. Bind yourself; in these days you will, with delight, see my arts. I'll give you what no human has ever seen.

FAUST. What can you, poor devil, give? Was a human spirit, in its high striving, ever grasped by your kind? Yet you have food that does not satisfy, you have red gold that, restless as quicksilver, runs out of your hand, a game in which one never wins, a girl who, on my breast, is already pledging herself with sidelong glances to the next man, the lovely divine joy of honor that vanishes like a meteor. Show me the fruit that rots before one picks it, and trees that grow new green every day!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Such a commission doesn't frighten me. With such treasures I can serve. But, good friend, the time is also approaching when we may peacefully feast on something good.

FAUST. If ever I lay myself, contented, on a bed of sloth, then it's all over with me at once! If ever you can flatter me with a lie that I might please myself, if you can deceive me with enjoyment — let that be my last day! That's the wager I offer!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Done!

FAUST. And shake on it! If ever I say to the moment: "Stay, you are so fair!" — then you may put me in chains, then I will gladly perish! Then let the death-bell ring; then you are released from your service. The clock may stop, the hand may fall, time will be over for me!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Consider it well — we will not forget.
FAUST. To that you have full right. I haven't presumed wantonly. As I persist, I am a slave — yours or whoever's, what does it matter to me?
MEPHISTOPHELES. I will, today already, at the doctoral feast, fulfill my duty as servant. Just one thing! For life or death's sake, I beg of you a few lines.

FAUST. Do you, pedant, demand something in writing too? Have you never known a man, never known a man's word? Is it not enough that my spoken word should command my days for eternity? Doesn't the world rage on in all its currents, and a promise is supposed to hold me fast? Yet this delusion is set in our hearts; who would gladly be free of it? Blessed is he who carries pure faithfulness in his bosom — no sacrifice will he ever regret! But a parchment, written and stamped, is a specter from which everyone shrinks. The word dies already in the pen; wax and leather rule. What do you, evil spirit, want of me? Bronze, marble, parchment, paper? Should I write with stylus, chisel, pen? I leave the choice entirely to you.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Why exaggerate your oratory so heatedly all at once? Any little scrap will do. You sign yourself with a little drop of blood.
FAUST. If this entirely satisfies you, then let it stay with this farce.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Blood is a quite particular juice.

FAUST. Have no fear that I'll break this bond! The striving of all my power is precisely what I promise. I have puffed myself up too high; only your rank is fit for me. The great spirit scorned me; nature locks herself away from me. The thread of thought is torn; I have long been disgusted with all knowing. In the depths of sensuality let us still glowing passions! Let every wonder stand at once ready in unpenetrated magic veils! Let us throw ourselves into the rush of time, into the rolling of events! Pain and pleasure, success and frustration, may then alternate as they will; only restless activity makes the man.
MEPHISTOPHELES. No measure or goal is set for you. If you'd like to nibble everywhere, snatch something in flight, may what gives you joy do you good. Just grab and don't be shy!

FAUST. You hear: there's no question of joy. To frenzy I dedicate myself, to the most painful enjoyment, to enamored hatred, refreshing vexation. My breast, healed of the urge for knowledge, shall in future close itself off from no pain, and what is allotted to all of mankind I will enjoy in my innermost self, with my mind grasp the highest and deepest, heap their weal and woe on my breast — and so expand my own self into their selves, and at the end, like them, founder.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Oh, believe me, I who have chewed for many thousand years on this hard food, that from cradle to grave no man has digested the old sourdough! Believe one of my kind: this whole thing is made for one God! He finds himself in eternal splendor; us he has brought into the darkness, and you can use only day and night.
FAUST. But I will!

MEPHISTOPHELES. That's something to hear! Yet only one thing worries me: time is short, art is long. I should think you might let yourself be taught. Associate yourself with a poet, let the gentleman roam in thought and heap all noble qualities on your honored crown — the lion's courage, the stag's swiftness, the Italian's fiery blood, the North's endurance. Let him discover for you the secret of joining magnanimity and cunning, and falling in love, with warm youthful drives, according to a plan. I'd like to know such a gentleman myself — I would call him Sir Microcosm.
FAUST. What am I, then, if it's not possible to attain the crown of mankind, toward which all senses press?
MEPHISTOPHELES. You are at the end — what you are. Put on wigs of a million curls, set your foot in towering platforms, you still remain what you are.

FAUST. I feel it: in vain I have heaped on myself all the treasures of the human spirit, and when at the end I sit down, no new strength wells up within. I am not a hair's breadth higher, am no closer to the Infinite.

MEPHISTOPHELES. My good sir, you see things just as people happen to see them. We must do this more cleverly, before the joy of life flees from us. What the devil — yes, hands and feet, head and arse, those are yours; but everything I freshly enjoy, is that any the less mine? If I can pay for six stallions, are their powers not mine? I race along and am a real man, as if I had four-and-twenty legs. So briskly! Let all this brooding go, and right out into the world! I tell you: a fellow who speculates is like an animal on a barren heath, led around in a circle by an evil spirit, while all around lies fine green pasture.
FAUST. How shall we begin?

MEPHISTOPHELES. We're just leaving. What kind of a torture-place is this? What kind of life is it, this — boring yourself and the boys? Leave that to Sir Neighbor Paunch! Why do you bother to thresh the straw? The best of what you can know, you can't tell the lads anyway. I hear one of them in the corridor now!
FAUST. It's not possible for me to see him.
MEPHISTOPHELES. The poor lad has been waiting long; he can't be sent away uncomforted. Come, give me your gown and cap; the costume must look excellent on me.
[He changes clothes.]
Now leave it to my wit! I only need a quarter of an hour. Meanwhile prepare yourself for the lovely journey!
[Exit FAUST. MEPHISTOPHELES in FAUST's long gown.]

Just despise reason and science, mankind's very highest power. Just let the lying spirit confirm you in dazzlement and magic-tricks, and I have you absolutely. Fate has given him a spirit that, untamed, always presses forward, whose hasty striving leaps over the joys of the earth. I'll drag him through wild life, through flat insignificance. He shall flounder, stiffen, stick fast for me, and to his insatiability food and drink shall float before greedy lips. He'll beg in vain for refreshment, and even if he hadn't given himself over to the devil, he'd still have to perish!
[A STUDENT enters.] STUDENT.
I have been here only a short time, and come full of devotion to speak with and meet a man of whom everyone tells me with reverence.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Your courtesy delights me very much! You see a man like many another. Have you looked around elsewhere yet?
STUDENT. I beg you, take me on! I come with all good will, decent money, and fresh blood. My mother could hardly let me go. I would gladly learn something proper out here.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Then you've come to just the right place.

STUDENT. Honestly, I'd like to be off again already. In these walls, in these halls, I'm not at all happy. The space is so cramped; one sees nothing green, no tree. And in the lecture rooms, on the benches, my hearing, sight, and thinking all desert me.

MEPHISTOPHELES. That's only a matter of habit. So a child does not at first take willingly to its mother's breast — but soon nourishes itself with delight. So at the breasts of wisdom, your appetite will grow with each day.
STUDENT. I'll hang on her neck with joy — but tell me only, how do I get there?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Declare yourself, before you go any further: which faculty do you choose?
STUDENT. I would like to become truly learned, and would gladly grasp what is on earth and in heaven, science and nature.
MEPHISTOPHELES. There you're on the right track; only you must not let yourself be distracted.
STUDENT. I'm in it heart and soul; though, of course, I would also enjoy a little freedom and pleasure on fine summer holidays.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Use the time, it slips away so fast — but order teaches you how to win time. My dear friend, I therefore advise you: first, Collegium Logicum. There your mind will be properly broken in, laced into Spanish boots, so that thereafter it may creep along the path of thought more circumspectly, and won't go zigzagging hither and thither like a will-o'-the-wisp. Then for many a day they teach you that what you used to do at one stroke — like eating and drinking, freely — needs One! Two! Three! to be done. To be sure, with the factory of thought it's like a master weaver's piece, where one tread sets a thousand threads in motion, the shuttles shoot back and forth, the threads flow unseen, one stroke makes a thousand connections. The philosopher steps in and proves to you it had to be so: the first was thus, the second thus, and therefore the third and fourth thus. And if the first and second were not, the third and fourth would never be. Pupils everywhere praise this — but they have not become weavers. Whoever wants to know and describe a living thing first tries to drive the spirit out of it. Then he has the parts in his hand — only, alas, the spiritual bond is missing. Encheiresin naturae [the handling of nature], chemistry calls it, mocking herself and not knowing how.
STUDENT. I can't quite follow you.
MEPHISTOPHELES. That will get better soon enough, when you learn to reduce everything and properly classify.
STUDENT. With all of this I get so dizzy, as if a millwheel were going round in my head.

MEPHISTOPHELES. After that, before all other things, you must apply yourself to metaphysics! There see to it that you grasp profoundly what does not fit into the human brain. For what goes in and what doesn't, a splendid word is at your service. But for now, this half-year, observe the strictest order. Five hours you have each day; be inside at the stroke of the bell! Have prepared yourself well beforehand, studied the paragraphs well, so that you may afterward see better that he says nothing other than what's in the book. Yet apply yourself to the writing — as if the Holy Spirit were dictating to you!
STUDENT. You won't have to tell me that twice! I see how useful it is — for what one possesses in black on white, one can carry confidently home.
MEPHISTOPHELES. But choose me a faculty!
STUDENT. Jurisprudence I cannot bring myself to take.

MEPHISTOPHELES. I cannot blame you too much for that. I know how it stands with this discipline. Laws and rights are inherited like an eternal sickness; they drag themselves from generation to generation, and quietly shift from place to place. Reason becomes nonsense, kindness becomes a plague. Woe to you that you are a grandchild! Of the right that is born with us — of that, alas, there is never a word.
STUDENT. My disgust is increased by you. Oh happy he whom you instruct! I'd almost like to study theology now.

MEPHISTOPHELES. I shouldn't wish to mislead you. As for this science: it is so hard to avoid the wrong path; so much hidden poison lies in it, that it can hardly be distinguished from medicine. Best here too, to listen to only one master, and swear by the master's words. On the whole — stick to words! Then you walk through the safe gate into the temple of certainty.
STUDENT. But there must be a concept attached to the word.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Just so! Only one mustn't torture oneself too anxiously. For just where concepts are missing, a word inserts itself at the right time. With words one can argue brilliantly, with words prepare a system, in words one can excellently believe — from a word not a jot can be stolen.

STUDENT. Forgive me, I keep you with so many questions, but I must trouble you still further. Won't you tell me a powerful little word about medicine too? Three years is a short time, and, God! the field is far too wide. If one has only a hint, one feels one's way better afterward.
MEPHISTOPHELES [aside]. I'm sick now of the dry tone — I must really play the devil again.
[Aloud.]

The spirit of medicine is easy to grasp. You study the great world and the small, only in the end to let it go as it pleases God. In vain you wander far and wide in scientific pursuit; each only learns what he can learn. But the one who seizes the moment — that is the right man. You're still pretty well built; you won't lack boldness either, and if you only trust yourself, the other souls will trust you. Above all, learn to manage women. Their eternal aches and sighs in their thousand forms are to be cured from one single point — and if you act half-decently, you have them all under your hat. A title must first make them confide in you, that your art surpasses many arts. As a welcome, you then grope for all those little items for which another spends many years; understand well how to press the little pulse, and grasp them, with fiery sly glances, freely about the slender hip — to see how tightly they are laced.
STUDENT. Now this looks better! At least one sees where and how.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Gray, dear friend, is all theory, and green is the golden tree of life.
STUDENT. I swear to you, it's like a dream to me. Might I trouble you another time, to hear your wisdom to its depths?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Whatever I can, I'll gladly do.
STUDENT. I really cannot leave again — I must still hand you my album. Grant me your favor with this token!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Very well.
[He writes and gives it back.]
STUDENT [reads]. Eritis sicut Deus, scientes bonum et malum. ["You shall be as God, knowing good and evil."]
[He closes it reverently and takes his leave.]
MEPHISTOPHELES. Just follow the old saying and my cousin the Snake — your god-likeness will surely give you grief one day!
[FAUST enters.] FAUST.
Where shall we go now?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Wherever you please. We'll see the small world, then the great. With what joy, with what profit, will you sponge your way through the course!
FAUST. But, with my long beard, I lack the easy manner. The attempt won't succeed for me. I never knew how to fit myself into the world; before others I feel so small. I'll always be at a loss.
MEPHISTOPHELES. My good friend, all that will sort itself out. As soon as you trust yourself, you'll know how to live.
FAUST. But how do we get out of the house? Where do you have horses, servant, carriage?

MEPHISTOPHELES. We just spread out the cloak — it will carry us through the air. Just take no large bundle on this bold step. A bit of fiery air, which I'll prepare, will lift us nimbly from this earth. And if we are light, the ascent goes quickly. I congratulate you on your new course of life!

chapters.title: Auerbach's Cellar in Leipzig
paragraphs: FROSCH. That's your fault — you bring nothing, not a single bit of foolery, no smut at all.
FROSCH
[pours a glass of wine over his head.]
There — you have both!
BRANDER. Twice a swine!
FROSCH. You wanted it — one should be one!
SIEBEL. Out the door, whoever quarrels! With open chest sing the round, swill and shout! Up! Holla! Ho!
ALTMAYER. Woe is me, I'm done for! Cotton wool here! The fellow is splitting my ears.
SIEBEL. When the vault echoes, only then do you really feel the bass-tone's primal force.
FROSCH. That's right — out with anyone who takes offense! Ah! tara lara da!
ALTMAYER. Ah! tara lara da!
FROSCH. The throats are tuned.
[Sings.]
The dear, holy Roman Empire — how does it still hold together?

BRANDER. A nasty song! Phooey! A political song! A wretched song! Thank God every morning that you don't have to worry about the Roman Empire! At least I count it a generous gain that I am not Emperor or Chancellor. But we too must not be without a head; let us elect a pope. You know what quality tips the scale, lifts the man.
FROSCH [sings]. Soar up, Lady Nightingale, greet my sweetheart for me ten thousand times.
SIEBEL. No greeting to my sweetheart! I will hear nothing of it!
FROSCH. Greeting and kiss to my sweetheart! You won't deny me that!
[Sings.]
Bolt up! In the still night. Bolt up! The dearest one is awake. Bolt down! Early in the morning.

SIEBEL. Yes, sing, just sing, and praise her and extol her! In my time I will laugh too. She has cheated me; she'll do the same to you. As her sweetheart let her be granted a goblin! Let him flirt with her at a crossroads. An old billy-goat, returning from the Brocken, may bleat "good night" to her at full gallop! A decent fellow of real flesh and blood is far too good for the wench. I will have nothing to do with greetings, except to smash in her windows!

BRANDER [striking the table]. Pay attention! Pay attention! Listen to me! Gentlemen, admit it: I know how to live. People in love sit here, and to these I must, as my standing requires, give a proper good-night song. Pay attention! A song in the very latest style! And join in the refrain with vigor!
[He sings.]

There was a rat in the cellar nest, lived only on fat and butter, had grown itself a paunch like Doctor Luther. The cook had set out poison for it; then the world grew so cramped for it, as if it had love in its body.
CHORUS [exulting]. As if it had love in its body.
