BRANDER. It tore around, it dashed outside, drank from every puddle, gnawed and clawed up the whole house — its raging was no use at all. Many an anxious leap it made, soon the poor creature had enough, as if it had love in its body.
CHORUS. As if it had love in its body.

BRANDER. Driven by terror in broad daylight, it ran toward the kitchen, fell at the hearth, twitched and lay there, and gasped pitifully. Then the poisoner laughed: Ha! she's whistling on her last leg, as if she had love in her body.
CHORUS. As if she had love in her body.
SIEBEL. How the simple lads enjoy themselves! It's a fine art, I must say, to scatter poison for poor rats!
BRANDER. They stand high in your favor, do they?
ALTMAYER. The pot-belly with the bald patch! Misfortune makes him tame and mild; he sees in the swollen rat his quite natural likeness.
[Enter FAUST and MEPHISTOPHELES.] MEPHISTOPHELES.

Now, before all else, I must bring you into merry company, so you may see how easily one can live. For these folk, every day is a feast. With little wit and much complacency, each one spins in a tight circle dance, like young cats with their tails. As long as they don't complain of headaches, as long as the innkeeper still gives credit, they are content and untroubled.
BRANDER. They've just come from a journey, you can see it in their odd manner; they've not been here an hour.
FROSCH. Truly, you're right! Leipzig is the place for me! It's a little Paris, and shapes its people.
SIEBEL. What do you take the strangers for?
FROSCH. Just let me at them! With a full glass I can pull the worms out of those fellows' noses as easily as a child's tooth. They seem to me from a noble house — they look proud and discontented.
BRANDER. Mountebanks, for sure, I'll bet!
ALTMAYER. Perhaps.
FROSCH. Watch — I'll screw it out of them.
MEPHISTOPHELES [to FAUST]. The little folk never sense the devil, even when he has them by the collar.
FAUST. Greetings, gentlemen!
SIEBEL. Many thanks for your greeting in return.
[Quietly, looking sideways at MEPHISTOPHELES.]
Why does that fellow limp on one foot?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Are we permitted to sit with you? Instead of the good drink one cannot get, may the company entertain us.
ALTMAYER. You seem a very particular man.
FROSCH. You set out late from Rippach, perhaps? Did you sup tonight first with Master Hans?
MEPHISTOPHELES. We rode past him today; we spoke with him last time. He had much to tell about his cousins, and gave us many greetings to deliver to each one.
[He bows to FROSCH.]
ALTMAYER [softly].
There you have it! He understands the joke!
SIEBEL. A crafty rascal!
FROSCH. Just wait, I'll catch him yet!
MEPHISTOPHELES. If I'm not mistaken, we heard practiced voices singing chorus? Surely song must echo splendidly here from this vault!
FROSCH. Are you, by chance, a virtuoso?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Oh no! The power is weak, but the desire is great.
ALTMAYER. Give us a song!
MEPHISTOPHELES. As many as you wish.
SIEBEL. But it must be a brand-new piece!
MEPHISTOPHELES. We've just come back from Spain, the lovely land of wine and song.
[Sings.]
There was once a king, who had a great flea —
FROSCH. Listen! A flea! Did you catch that? A flea is a tidy guest indeed.

MEPHISTOPHELES [sings]. There was once a king, who had a great flea, whom he loved not a little, just like his own son. He called for his tailor; the tailor came hurrying. Cut me clothes for the young squire, and measure him for breeches!
BRANDER. Don't forget to impress on the tailor that he measure most precisely, and that, as he loves his head, the breeches throw no creases!

MEPHISTOPHELES. In velvet and in silk he was now arrayed, had ribbons on his coat, also a cross upon it, and was at once a minister, with a great star. Then his brothers and sisters at court became great lords too.

And lords and ladies at court were sorely tormented; the queen and her ladies-in-waiting were stung and gnawed, and they were not allowed to crush them, nor scratch them off. We crush and choke them at once, though, when one stings.
CHORUS [exulting]. We crush and choke them at once, though, when one stings.
FROSCH. Bravo! Bravo! That was fine!
SIEBEL. So may every flea fare!
BRANDER. Sharpen the fingers and pinch them neatly!
ALTMAYER. Long live freedom! Long live wine!
MEPHISTOPHELES. I would gladly drink a glass to honor freedom highly, if your wines were just a little better.
SIEBEL. We don't want to hear that again!
MEPHISTOPHELES. I only fear the innkeeper might object — otherwise I would treat these worthy guests to something from our own cellar.
SIEBEL. Just bring it on! I'll take it on myself.
FROSCH. If you provide a good glass, we'll praise you for it. Just don't give too small a sample — for if I'm to judge, I demand a real mouthful.
ALTMAYER [softly]. They're from the Rhine, I sense.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Get me a gimlet!
BRANDER. What's that for? You don't have the casks at the door, do you?
ALTMAYER. The innkeeper has a basket of tools back there.
MEPHISTOPHELES [takes the gimlet]. [to FROSCH]
Now tell me, what would you like to taste?
FROSCH. What do you mean? Have you so many kinds?
MEPHISTOPHELES. I leave it to each man's choice.
ALTMAYER [to FROSCH]. Aha! You're already starting to lick your lips.
FROSCH. Good! If I'm to choose, I'll have Rhine wine. The fatherland yields the very best gifts.
MEPHISTOPHELES [as he bores a hole in the table-edge at the place where FROSCH sits].
Get a bit of wax to make stoppers at once!
ALTMAYER. Ah, that's conjurer's stuff.
MEPHISTOPHELES [to BRANDER]. And you?
BRANDER. I want champagne wine — and good and sparkling it must be!
MEPHISTOPHELES [bores; meanwhile someone has made the wax stoppers and plugged the holes].
BRANDER. One can't always avoid foreign things; the good often lies so far from us. A true German man can't stand a Frenchman, but he gladly drinks their wines.
SIEBEL [as MEPHISTOPHELES approaches his place].
I must confess, I don't care for the dry sort — give me a glass of the genuine sweet!
MEPHISTOPHELES [bores]. For you, Tokay shall flow at once.
ALTMAYER. No, gentlemen, look me in the face! I see clearly, you're only making fools of us.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Hey! Hey! With such noble guests it would be venturing rather a lot. Quick! Just say it straight out! With which wine can I serve you?
ALTMAYER. With any! Just no more questions.
[After all the holes have been bored and plugged.]

MEPHISTOPHELES [with strange gestures]. Grapes the vine bears! Horns the billy-goat. The wine is juicy, wood are the vines, the wooden table can give wine too. A deep look into nature! Here is a wonder — only believe!
Now pull the stoppers and enjoy!
ALL [as they pull out the stoppers, and the wine each requested runs into his glass].
O lovely fountain, that flows for us!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Only take care that you don't spill any!
[They drink repeatedly.]
ALL [singing]. We feel quite cannibalishly fine, like five hundred sows!
MEPHISTOPHELES. The folk are free — see how well they're doing!
FAUST. I'd be inclined to leave now.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Just watch first — bestiality will reveal itself most splendidly.
SIEBEL [drinks carelessly; the wine spills onto the floor and turns to flame].
Help! Fire! Help! Hell is burning!
MEPHISTOPHELES [addressing the flame]. Be still, friendly element!
[to the company.]
For this time it was only a drop of purgatorial fire. SIEBEL.
What's this supposed to be? Wait! You'll pay dear for this! It seems you don't know us.
FROSCH. Don't let him do that to us a second time!
ALTMAYER. I'd say we should tell him quietly to clear off.
SIEBEL. What, sir? You'd presume to carry on your hocus-pocus here?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Quiet, you old wine-cask!
SIEBEL. Broomstick! You'd treat us rudely on top of it?
BRANDER. Just wait! Blows shall rain down.
ALTMAYER [pulls a stopper from the table; fire springs out at him].
I'm burning! I'm burning!
SIEBEL. Sorcery! Strike! The fellow is outlawed!
[They draw their knives and go for MEPHISTOPHELES.]
MEPHISTOPHELES [with grave gesture]. False image and word, change sense and place! Be here and there!
[They stand astonished and look at one another.]
ALTMAYER. Where am I? What lovely country!
FROSCH. Vineyards! Do I see right?
SIEBEL. And grapes within reach!
BRANDER. Here under this green leaf, see what a stalk! See what a cluster!
[He grabs SIEBEL by the nose. The others do the same to each other and raise their knives.]
MEPHISTOPHELES [as before]. Error, let go the band of the eyes! And mark how the devil makes sport.
[He vanishes with FAUST. The fellows spring apart.]
SIEBEL. What's going on?
ALTMAYER. What?
FROSCH. Was that your nose?
BRANDER [to SIEBEL].
And I have yours in my hand!
ALTMAYER. It was a blow that went through every limb! Bring a chair, I'm sinking down!
FROSCH. No, just tell me, what happened?
SIEBEL. Where is the fellow? If I track him down, he won't get away alive!
ALTMAYER. I myself saw him out at the cellar door — riding on a wine-cask. — My feet feel heavy as lead.
[Turning toward the table.]
Goodness! Could the wine still be flowing?
SIEBEL. It was all a fraud, lies and illusion.
FROSCH. Yet to me it was as if I were drinking wine.
BRANDER. But what about the grapes?
ALTMAYER. Now tell me — they say one shouldn't believe in miracles!

chapters.title: Witch's Kitchen
paragraphs: FAUST. This crazy magic-business repels me! Do you promise me I'll be cured in this welter of frenzy? Am I to seek advice from an old hag? And will the slop-cookery shave thirty years off my body? Woe to me, if you know nothing better! Hope has already vanished from me. Has nature, has any noble spirit, not discovered some balsam somewhere?
MEPHISTOPHELES. My friend, now you're talking sensibly again! There is also a natural means to make you young; only it stands in another book, and is a strange chapter.
FAUST. I want to know it.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Good! A means without money, doctor, and sorcery: take yourself out at once into the fields; begin to hoe and dig; keep yourself and your mind within a quite limited circle; nourish yourself on unmixed food; live with the cattle as cattle, and don't think it robbery to dung the field you yourself reap. That's the best means, believe me, to keep you young into your eighties!
FAUST. I'm not used to that — I can't bring myself to take a spade in hand. The narrow life doesn't suit me at all.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Then the witch will have to do it.
FAUST. Why just that old woman? Can't you brew the drink yourself?

MEPHISTOPHELES. That would be a fine pastime! I would build a thousand bridges in the meantime. Not art and science alone — patience must go into the work. A quiet spirit busies itself for years; only time makes the fine fermentation strong. And everything that goes into it — they're truly wondrous things! The devil taught her the recipe, true; but the devil himself can't make it.
[Catching sight of the Animals.]
Look — what a graceful tribe! That's the maid! That's the man-servant!
[To the Animals.]
It seems the mistress is not at home?
THE ANIMALS. At a feast, out of the house and up the chimney!
MEPHISTOPHELES. How long does she usually go gallivanting?
THE ANIMALS. As long as we warm our paws.
MEPHISTOPHELES [to FAUST]. How do you find these tender creatures?
FAUST. As insipid as anyone I ever saw!
MEPHISTOPHELES. No, a discourse like this is just the kind I most prefer to hold!
[To the Animals.]
Tell me then, you cursed dolls! What are you stirring there in the slop?
ANIMALS. We're cooking thin beggar's-soup.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Then you have a great public.
THE TOMCAT
[comes forward and fawns on MEPHISTOPHELES.]
Oh, just throw the dice, and make me rich, and let me win! Things stand badly, and if I had money, I'd have my wits.
MEPHISTOPHELES. How happy the ape would consider himself, if he could only play the lottery!
[Meanwhile the young monkeys have been playing with a great ball and roll it forward.]

THE TOMCAT. That's the world; it rises and falls and rolls constantly; it rings like glass — how soon does that break? It's hollow inside; here it gleams brightly, and here even more, I am alive! My dear son, keep away from it! You must die! It's made of clay; there will be shards.
MEPHISTOPHELES. What's that sieve for?
THE TOMCAT [fetching it down]. If you were a thief, I'd recognize you at once.
[He runs to the cat and lets her look through it.]
Look through the sieve! Do you recognize the thief — and dare not name him?
MEPHISTOPHELES [approaching the fire]. And this pot?
TOMCAT and CAT. The silly fool! He doesn't know the pot, he doesn't know the cauldron!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Discourteous beast!
THE TOMCAT. Take this fly-whisk here, and seat yourself in the armchair!
[He urges MEPHISTOPHELES to sit.]
FAUST [who has been standing all this while before a mirror, now drawing close to it, now stepping back from it].

What do I see? What heavenly image shows itself in this magic mirror! O Love, lend me the swiftest of your wings, and lead me to her realm! Ah, if I don't stay where I am, if I dare to step closer, I can only see her as if through a mist! — The most beautiful image of a woman! Is it possible — is woman so beautiful? Must I see in this body, stretched out, the very essence of every heaven? Is such a thing to be found on earth?

MEPHISTOPHELES. Naturally — when a god toils for six days and even at the end says "Bravo!", something clever has to come of it. For this time, look till you've had your fill. I know how to track down such a treasure for you, and blessed is he who has the good fortune to lead her home as bridegroom!
[FAUST keeps gazing into the mirror. MEPHISTOPHELES, stretching in the chair and playing with the fly-whisk, continues speaking.]
Here I sit like a king on his throne; I hold the scepter here, only the crown is missing.
THE ANIMALS [which up till now have been making all kinds of strange motions among themselves, bring MEPHISTOPHELES a crown with great shouting].
Oh, would you be so good — with sweat and with blood, glue the crown together!
[They handle the crown clumsily and break it into two pieces, with which they leap about.]
Now it's done! We talk and we see, we hear and we rhyme;
FAUST [facing the mirror]. Woe is me! I'm nearly going mad.
MEPHISTOPHELES [pointing to the animals]. Now my own head almost begins to swim.
THE ANIMALS. And if it succeeds for us, and if it fits — they are thoughts!
FAUST [as before]. My breast begins to burn! Let's get away quickly!
MEPHISTOPHELES [in the same posture]. Well, at least one must admit that they are sincere poets.
[The cauldron, which the cat has been neglecting, begins to boil over; a great flame springs up and shoots out of the chimney. The WITCH comes down through the flame with terrible shrieks.]
THE WITCH. Ow! Ow! Ow! Ow! Damned beast! Cursed sow! You neglect the cauldron, you scorch the mistress! Cursed beast!
[Catching sight of FAUST and MEPHISTOPHELES.]
What's this here? Who are you here? What do you want? Who has crept in? May the fiery torment go to your bones!
[She thrusts the foam-spoon into the cauldron and sprays flames at FAUST, MEPHISTOPHELES, and the animals. The animals whimper.]
MEPHISTOPHELES [turns the fly-whisk he holds in his hand and strikes about among the glasses and pots].
Smashed! Smashed! There lies the gruel! There lies the glass! It's only a joke — the time, you carrion, to your melody.
[As the witch steps back full of rage and horror.]

Don't you recognize me? Skeleton! You monster! Don't you recognize your lord and master? What holds me back from striking — smashing you and your cat-spirits? Have you no more respect for the red doublet? Can't you recognize the cock's feather? Have I disguised this face? Should I name myself, perhaps?
THE WITCH. Oh sir, forgive the rough greeting! I didn't see a horse's foot. Where then are your two ravens?

MEPHISTOPHELES. This time you got off lightly. After all, it's been a while since we've seen each other. Culture, which licks all the world clean, has reached the devil too. The Nordic phantom is no longer to be seen — where do you see horns, tail, and claws? And as for the foot, which I cannot do without — that would harm me among people. So I, like many a young man, have for many years made use of false calves.
THE WITCH [dancing]. I lose all sense and reason at the sight of young Squire Satan here again!
MEPHISTOPHELES. That name, woman, I forbid!
THE WITCH. Why? What has it done to you?

MEPHISTOPHELES. It's long since written into the book of fables; though men are no better off — they're rid of the Evil One, the evil ones remain. Call me Sir Baron, then the matter is in order. I am a cavalier, like other cavaliers. You don't doubt my noble blood; here, this is the coat of arms I bear!
[He makes an indecent gesture.]
THE WITCH [laughing immoderately]. Ha! Ha! That's just like you! You're a rogue, just as you always were!
MEPHISTOPHELES [to FAUST]. My friend, learn this well! This is the way to deal with witches.
THE WITCH. Now tell me, gentlemen, what you require.
MEPHISTOPHELES. A good glass of the well-known juice! But I must ask you for the oldest; the years double its strength.
THE WITCH. Gladly! Here I have a bottle that I myself sometimes nip from, that no longer stinks in the slightest; I'll gladly give you a little glass.
[Quietly.]
But if this man drinks it unprepared, he can't, as you well know, live another hour.
MEPHISTOPHELES. He's a good friend, who shall thrive on it; I gladly grant him the best of your kitchen. Draw your circle, speak your spells, and give him a cupful!

THE WITCH [with strange gestures, draws a circle and places wondrous things inside it; meanwhile the glasses begin to ring, the cauldron to sound, and they make music. Finally she brings a great book, places the monkeys in the circle, where they serve her as a desk and must hold the torch. She beckons FAUST to step over to her.]
FAUST [to MEPHISTOPHELES]. No, tell me, what is this supposed to be? The crazy stuff, the frenzied gestures, the most insipid fraud — I know all this, and find it hateful enough.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Eh, nonsense! It's only for laughs. Don't be so stern! She must, as a doctor, perform some hocus-pocus, so that the juice may thrive in you.
[He urges FAUST to step into the circle.]
[The WITCH, with great emphasis, begins to declaim from the book.]

You must understand! Of one make ten, and let two go, and make three even, and you are rich. Lose the four! From five and six — so says the witch — make seven and eight, and it's accomplished: and nine is one, and ten is none. That is the witch's one-times-one!
FAUST. The old woman seems to be talking in fever.

MEPHISTOPHELES. That's far from over yet — I know it well, the whole book runs like that. I've wasted plenty of time on it; for a perfect contradiction stays equally mysterious to the wise as to fools. My friend, the art is old and new. It was the way at all times to spread error instead of truth, by three and one and one and three. So they prattle and teach undisturbed; who wants to bother with the fools? Usually a man, if he only hears words, believes there must be something thinkable in them.
THE WITCH [continues]. The high power of science, hidden from the whole world! And whoever does not think — to him it is given as a gift; he has it without trouble.
FAUST. What nonsense is she reciting to us? My head is about to break. I think I hear a whole chorus of a hundred thousand fools speaking.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Enough, enough, splendid sibyl! Bring on your drink, and quickly fill the cup to the brim; for this draught will not harm my friend: he is a man of many degrees, who has taken many a good gulp.
THE WITCH [with many ceremonies, pours the drink into a cup; as she brings it to FAUST's lips, a small flame springs up].
MEPHISTOPHELES. Briskly down with it! Keep going! It will gladden your heart at once. You're on intimate terms with the devil, and you'd shrink from the flame?
[The WITCH dissolves the circle. FAUST steps out.]
MEPHISTOPHELES. Now briskly out! You mustn't rest.
THE WITCH. May the little draught do you good!
MEPHISTOPHELES [to the WITCH]. And if I can do you any favor, just let me know on Walpurgis Night.
THE WITCH. Here is a song! If you sing it now and then, you will feel a particular effect.

MEPHISTOPHELES [to FAUST]. Come quickly and let yourself be led; you must necessarily perspire, so that the power can penetrate inside and out. I'll teach you afterward to value noble idleness, and soon you'll feel with intimate delight how Cupid stirs and leaps about.
FAUST. Let me look quickly into the mirror once more! The image of the woman was far too beautiful!
MEPHISTOPHELES. No! No! You shall soon see, in the flesh before you, the model of all women.
[Aside.] You'll see, with this drink in your body, soon Helen in every woman.

chapters.title: Street
paragraphs: MARGARET. I'm neither lady nor pretty, and can go home unescorted.
[She pulls free and exits.]

FAUST. By heaven, this child is beautiful! I've never seen anything like her. She's so modest, so virtuous — and at the same time a little tart. The red of her lip, the light of her cheek — to my dying day I won't forget! The way she lowered her eyes is stamped deep on my heart; the way she was so curt — that is utter delight!
[Enter MEPHISTOPHELES.] FAUST.
Listen, you must get me that girl!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Well, which?
FAUST. She just walked past.

MEPHISTOPHELES. That one? She came from her priest, who absolved her of all her sins. I crept right up by the chair — she's a thoroughly innocent thing, who went to confession over nothing at all. Over her I have no power!
FAUST. She's over fourteen years old.
MEPHISTOPHELES. You're talking like Jack Loose-Liver, who wants every dear flower for himself, and fancies there's no honor or favor that's not for the picking — but it doesn't always work that way.
FAUST. My Master Praiseworthy, leave me in peace with the law! And I'll tell you straight: if that sweet young blood doesn't rest tonight in my arms, then we two part ways at midnight.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Consider what's possible! I need at least fourteen days just to scout out the opportunity.
FAUST. If I had seven hours of peace, I wouldn't need the devil to seduce a little creature like that.

MEPHISTOPHELES. You're already talking almost like a Frenchman. But I beg you, don't let it vex you: what good is enjoying it just like that? The pleasure is nowhere near as great as when, with all kinds of fuss, you knead and prepare the little doll, as many a foreign tale teaches.
FAUST. I have appetite enough without that.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Now, without insult and without joke: I tell you, with this lovely child it simply won't go quickly. Nothing's to be taken there by storm; we'll have to bend ourselves to cunning.
FAUST. Get me something of the angel's treasure! Lead me to her resting-place! Get me a kerchief from her breast, a garter for my love-lust!
MEPHISTOPHELES. So that you see I'll be useful and obliging in your pain — let's not lose a moment. I'll lead you into her room this very day.
FAUST. And shall I see her? Have her?
MEPHISTOPHELES. No! She'll be at a neighbor's. Meanwhile you can, all alone, feast yourself sated on the hope of all future joys, in her atmosphere.
FAUST. Can we go now?
MEPHISTOPHELES. It's still too early.
FAUST. Get me a present for her.
[Exit.]
MEPHISTOPHELES. A present already? Well done! He'll succeed! I know many a fine spot and many an old buried treasure; I must look around a bit.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Evening
paragraphs: MARGARET [plaiting and binding up her braids].
I'd give a lot if I only knew who that gentleman was today! He certainly looked very gallant, and is from a noble house — I could read it on his forehead — otherwise he wouldn't have been so bold.
[Exit.]
MEPHISTOPHELES. FAUST.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Come in, very softly, just come in!
FAUST [after some silence]. I beg you, leave me alone!
MEPHISTOPHELES [snooping about]. Not every girl keeps things so neat.
[Exit.]
FAUST [looking around].

Welcome, sweet twilight gleam, that weaves through this sanctuary! Seize my heart, you sweet pain of love, that lives, languishing, on the dew of hope! How everything around breathes the feeling of stillness, of order, of contentment! In this poverty, what fullness! In this dungeon, what bliss!
[He throws himself on the leather chair by the bed.]

Oh take me up, you who in the past received generations in your open arms in joy and sorrow! How often, ah, has a band of children clung around this fathers' throne! Perhaps, grateful for the holy Christ, my dear love here, with full child-cheeks, has piously kissed the withered hand of her grandfather. I feel, O girl, your spirit of fullness and order whispering around me — the spirit that motherly instructs you daily, that bids you spread the cloth cleanly on the table, even crinkle the sand at your feet. O dear hand! So godlike! Through you the cottage becomes a kingdom of heaven. And here!
[He lifts a bed-curtain.]

What rapturous awe seizes me! Here I'd linger for whole hours. Nature! Here, in light dreams, you formed the inborn angel; here lay the child! With warm life filling out the tender breast, and here, with holy pure weaving, the divine image worked itself out!
And you! What has brought you here? How deeply I feel myself moved! What do you want here? What weighs your heart down? Wretched Faust! I no longer know you.
Does a magic fragrance surround me here? I pressed in just to enjoy myself — and now I feel myself dissolving in a love-dream! Are we the plaything of every pressure of the air?
And if she were to step in this very moment, how you'd pay for your sacrilege! The great Hans — ah, how small! — would lie melted at her feet.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Quick! I see her coming below.
FAUST. Away! Away! I'll never come back!

MEPHISTOPHELES. Here's a casket, fairly heavy — I picked it up somewhere else. Just put it here in the cabinet. I swear to you, her senses will swim. I put little things inside to win another one. True, child is child, and play is play.
FAUST. I don't know — should I?

MEPHISTOPHELES. You ask so many questions? Perhaps you mean to keep the treasure? Then I advise your lust to spare the lovely time of day, and me the further trouble. I hope you're not stingy! I scratch my head, I rub my hands —
[He places the casket in the cabinet and locks it again.]

Just away! Quick! — to turn that sweet young child to your heart's wish and will. And you stand there as if you were heading into the lecture hall, as if Physics and Metaphysics stood bodily before you! Just away!
[Exit.]
MARGARET [with a lamp]. It's so close, so stuffy in here,
[She opens the window.]
and yet it's not so warm outside. I feel — I don't know how — I wish my mother would come home. A shudder runs over my body. I'm such a foolish, fearful woman!
[She begins to sing as she undresses.]
There was a king in Thule, faithful unto the grave, to whom his dying mistress gave a golden cup.
Nothing was dearer to him; he drained it at every feast, and his eyes overflowed each time he drank from it.
And when he came to die, he counted his cities in the realm, granted everything to his heir — but not the cup along with them.
He sat at the kingly feast, the knights around him, in the high ancestral hall, there in the castle by the sea.
There stood the old toper, drank his last glow of life, and threw the holy cup down into the flood.
He saw it tumbling, drinking, and sinking deep into the sea; his eyes too sank shut — he never drank a drop more.
[She opens the cabinet to put away her clothes, and sees the jewel-casket.]

How does this lovely casket get in here? I locked the cabinet for sure. It is wonderful! What might be inside? Perhaps someone brought it as a pledge, and my mother lent against it. There hangs a little key on a band — I think I'll open it! What is this? God in heaven! Look — I've never seen anything like it! Jewelry! With this, a noblewoman could go to the highest feast-day. How would the necklace look on me? Whose can this splendor be?
[She decks herself with it and steps before the mirror.]

If only the earrings were mine! One looks quite different at once. What good is beauty, young blood? It's all very well, but they let it all pass by; one is praised half out of pity. Toward gold throngs, on gold hangs everything. Ah, we poor ones!

chapters.title: Promenade
paragraphs: FAUST. What's the matter? What's pinching you so badly? I've never seen such a face in my life!
MEPHISTOPHELES. I'd give myself over to the devil at once, if I weren't a devil myself!
FAUST. Has something gone awry in your head? It suits you to rage like a madman!

MEPHISTOPHELES. Just think — the jewelry I got for Gretchen, a priest has carried off! — The mother got a look at the thing, and at once secretly grew uneasy: the woman has a very fine nose, always sniffing about in the prayer-book, and smelling at every piece of furniture whether the thing is sacred or profane. And on the jewelry she could smell clearly that there was not much blessing about it. "My child," she cried, "unjust goods catch the soul and consume the blood. Let's dedicate them to the Mother of God; she'll delight us with heaven's manna!" Little Margaret pulled a sour face — "It's a gift horse," she thought, "and truly, he is no godless man who brought it here so handsomely." The mother had a priest sent for; he had hardly heard the joke before he savored the sight thoroughly. He said: "That's the right disposition! He who overcomes wins. The Church has a good stomach, has eaten up whole countries and yet has never overstuffed herself; the Church alone, dear ladies, can digest unjust goods."
FAUST. That's a common practice — a Jew and a king can do it too.

MEPHISTOPHELES. He swept up brooch, chain, and rings as if they were so many mushrooms, thanked them no less and no more than if it had been a basket of nuts, promised them all heavenly reward — and they were greatly edified.
FAUST. And Gretchen?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Sits now restless, knows neither what she wants nor what she should do, thinks of the jewels day and night, and even more of the one who brought them to her.
FAUST. The dear one's grief pains me. Get her a new set at once! The first one was nothing much anyway.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Oh yes, to the gentleman it's all child's play!
FAUST. And do it — and arrange it to my mind! Get yourself attached to her neighbor. Be a devil for once and not a milksop, and bring some new jewelry over!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Yes, gracious sir, with all my heart.
[Exit FAUST.]
MEPHISTOPHELES. Such a lovesick fool sets off sun, moon, and all the stars for you in the air, just to amuse his sweetheart.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: The Neighbor's House
paragraphs: MARTHA. God forgive my dear husband — he hasn't done well by me! Goes straight off into the world, and leaves me alone on the straw. I truly didn't mean to grieve him; I loved him, God knows, with all my heart.
[She weeps.]
Perhaps he's even dead! — Oh, the pain! — If only I had a death certificate!
[MARGARET enters.] MARGARET.
Frau Martha!
MARTHA. Little Gretchen, what is it?
MARGARET. My knees nearly give way under me! I find another such casket in my cabinet, made of ebony — and things splendid through and through, far richer than the first.
MARTHA. She mustn't tell her mother about it; she'd carry it straight off to confession again.
MARGARET. Oh look, just look!
MARTHA [decking her with the jewels]. Oh, you blessed creature!
MARGARET. Alas, I can't be seen with this on the street, nor in the church.

MARTHA. Just come over to me often, and put the jewelry on here in secret. Walk back and forth before the looking-glass for an hour or so — we'll have our pleasure in it. And then there'll be an occasion, a feast, where one lets people see it bit by bit. A little chain first, then the pearl in the ear. The mother probably won't notice, and one can put her off with some excuse.
MARGARET. Whoever could have brought the two caskets? Things aren't going right!
[A knock.]
MARGARET. Oh God! Could that be my mother?
MARTHA [peeping through the curtain]. It's a strange gentleman — come in!
[Enter MEPHISTOPHELES.] MEPHISTOPHELES.
I'm so bold as to step right in — must beg the ladies' pardon.
[He steps back respectfully before MARGARET.]
I wished to ask for Frau Martha Schwerdtlein!
MARTHA. That's me — what does the gentleman have to say?
MEPHISTOPHELES [softly to her]. I know who you are now — that's enough for me; you have very distinguished company. Forgive the liberty I have taken; I'll come back this afternoon.
MARTHA [aloud]. Just think, child, of all the things in the world! The gentleman takes you for a young lady.
MARGARET. I am a poor young thing. Oh God! The gentleman is far too kind: jewelry and trinkets are not mine.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Ah, it's not the jewelry alone; she has a presence, a glance so sharp! How glad I am that I may stay.
MARTHA. So what news do you bring? I greatly desire —
MEPHISTOPHELES. I wish I had a happier piece of news! I hope you won't make me suffer for it: your husband is dead, and sends his greetings.
MARTHA. Dead? That faithful heart! Oh, woe! My husband is dead! Oh, I'm fainting!
MARGARET. Ah! Dear lady, do not despair!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Then hear the sad story!
MARGARET. Then I would not want to love a single day in my life — loss would grieve me to death.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Joy must have sorrow, sorrow must have joy.
MARTHA. Tell me how his life ended!
MEPHISTOPHELES. He lies buried in Padua, by Saint Anthony's, in a well-consecrated place, an everlasting cool resting-bed.
MARTHA. Have you nothing else to bring me?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Yes, a request, great and weighty: have three hundred Masses sung for him! Otherwise my pockets are empty.
MARTHA. What! Not one keepsake? No trinket? What every apprentice saves at the bottom of his sack, holds onto in remembrance, and would rather starve, would rather beg!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Madame, I'm sincerely sorry; but truly he didn't squander his money. He also bitterly regretted his faults — yes, and lamented his misfortune even more.
MARGARET. Ah, that people are so unhappy! Surely I will pray many a requiem for him.
MEPHISTOPHELES. You'd be worthy of stepping at once into marriage: you are a lovable child.
MARGARET. Oh no, that's not yet right.
MEPHISTOPHELES. If not a husband, then meanwhile a gallant. It's one of the greatest gifts of heaven, to have such a dear thing in your arms.
MARGARET. That's not the custom of this country.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Custom or not — it gets done all the same.
MARTHA. Tell me on!

MEPHISTOPHELES. I stood at his deathbed; it was something better than dung — half-rotten straw; but he died as a Christian, and found that he had still much more to settle on his account. "How," he cried, "must I hate myself from the bottom up, for so abandoning my trade and my wife! Ah, the memory kills me. If she would only forgive me even now in this life!" —
MARTHA [weeping]. The good man! I've long since forgiven him.
MEPHISTOPHELES. "But God knows — she was more to blame than I."
MARTHA. He's lying! What! to lie at the brink of the grave!

MEPHISTOPHELES. He certainly was rambling at his last gasp, if I'm even half a judge. "I had," he said, "no time to gape about for amusement — first children, then bread to make for them, and bread in the very widest sense, and I couldn't even eat my share in peace."
MARTHA. He forgot all loyalty, all love like that — the drudgery by day and night!

MEPHISTOPHELES. Not at all — he thought of you with all his heart. He said: "When I went away from Malta, I prayed fervently for wife and children; and heaven was good to us, so that our ship captured a Turkish vessel that carried a treasure of the great Sultan. There valor got its reward, and I received, as was due, my well-measured share of it."
MARTHA. Eh, what? Eh, where? Did he perhaps bury it?

MEPHISTOPHELES. Who knows where the four winds have it now? A pretty young lady took him under her wing, when he was wandering as a stranger in Naples; she did him so much love and faithfulness that he felt it to his blessed end.
MARTHA. The rogue! The thief — robbing his own children! Even all the misery, all the need, couldn't keep him from his shameful life!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Yes, look! For that he's now dead. If I were now in your place, I'd mourn him a chaste year, and meanwhile keep an eye out for a new treasure.

MARTHA. Oh God! Hard as my first one was, I'll not easily find another like him in this world! There could hardly be a more endearing little fool. He only loved too much wandering, and foreign women, and foreign wine, and that cursed dice-play.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Well, well — things might have stood and gone on if he had let you have about as much room on your side. I swear to you, on those terms I'd exchange the ring with you myself!
MARTHA. Oh, the gentleman's pleased to jest!
MEPHISTOPHELES [aside]. Now I'll be off in good time! She'd hold even the devil himself to his word.
[To GRETCHEN.]
And how does it stand with your heart?
MARGARET. What does the gentleman mean by that?
MEPHISTOPHELES [aside]. You good, innocent child!
[Aloud.]
Farewell, ladies!
MARGARET. Farewell!

MARTHA. Oh, tell me quickly! I'd like to have a certificate of where, how, and when my treasure died and was buried. I have always been a friend of order, and I'd like to read of his death in the weekly bulletin.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Yes, good lady, by two witnesses' mouths the truth is in any case made known. I have a fine companion, and I'll bring him before the magistrate. I'll bring him here.
MARTHA. Oh, do that, please!
MEPHISTOPHELES. And the young lady will be there too? — A fine fellow! He's traveled much, shows young ladies all courtesy.
MARGARET. I'd have to blush red before the gentleman.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Before no king on earth.
MARTHA. There behind the house in my garden, we'll await the gentlemen this evening.

chapters.title: Street
paragraphs: MEPHISTOPHELES. Ah, bravo! Do I find you on fire? In a short time Gretchen is yours. This evening you'll see her at neighbor Martha's. That's a woman as if specially picked for procuring and gypsy-business!
FAUST. Right!
MEPHISTOPHELES. But something is also required of us.
FAUST. One service is well worth another.
MEPHISTOPHELES. We just lodge a valid testimony that her husband's stretched-out limbs rest at a holy site in Padua.
FAUST. Very clever! We'll have to make the journey first!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Sancta simplicitas! [holy innocence!] That's not what's needed; just testify without knowing much.
FAUST. If you have nothing better, the plan's torn up.

MEPHISTOPHELES. O holy man! There you go! Is it the first time in your life you've borne false witness? Of God, of the world and what stirs in it, of man and what moves in his head and heart, haven't you given definitions with great force? With a brazen brow and a bold breast? And if you'll go really deep into it — you've known about all that, you must straight out admit it, just as much as about Herr Schwerdtlein's death!
FAUST. You are and remain a liar, a sophist.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Yes, if one didn't know a bit better. For tomorrow in all honor won't you fool poor Gretchen, and swear her all soul-love?
FAUST. And from the heart, at that.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Fine and good! Then there'll be eternal faithfulness and love, the one and only all-powerful drive — will that too come so straight from the heart?

FAUST. Stop that! It will! — When I feel, when I search for a name for the feeling, the tumult, and find none, then sweep through the world with all my senses, grasp at every loftiest word, and call this glow that burns me infinite, eternal, eternal — is that a devilish lying-game?
MEPHISTOPHELES. I'm right after all!

FAUST. Listen — note this — I beg you, and spare my lungs — whoever wants to be right and has only one tongue will be right for sure. So come on, I'm sick of chatter, since you are right, mainly because I must have it so.

chapters.title: Garden
paragraphs: FAUST. One look from you, one word — that delights me more than all the wisdom of this world.
[He kisses her hand.]
MARGARET. Don't trouble yourself! How can you kiss it? It's so ugly, so rough! What haven't I had to do already! My mother is far too particular.
[They walk past.]
MARTHA. And you, sir, you keep traveling on like that?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Ah, that business and duty drive us to it! With how much pain one leaves many a place — and yet at the moment one cannot stay!
MARTHA. In the swift years one can roam freely all about the world; but the bad time approaches, and to drag oneself, an old bachelor, alone to the grave — that has done no one any good.
MEPHISTOPHELES. With horror I see it from afar.
MARTHA. Therefore, dear sir, take counsel in time.
[They walk past.]
MARGARET. Yes, out of sight, out of mind! Politeness comes easily to you. But you have plenty of friends; they're more sensible than I am.
FAUST. O dearest, believe me — what people call sensible is often more vanity and shortsightedness.
MARGARET. How?
FAUST. Ah, that simplicity, that innocence, never recognizes itself and its holy worth! That humility, lowliness — the highest gifts of generously bestowing nature —
MARGARET. Just think of me a single moment, and I'll have time enough to think of you.
FAUST. You are alone a great deal?

MARGARET. Yes, our household is just small, and yet it has to be looked after. We have no maid; I have to cook, sweep, knit, and sew, and run from morning till night. And my mother is in every detail so exact! Not that she has to keep accounts so tight; we could afford ourselves more than others — my father left a tidy fortune, a little house and a little garden outside the city. But I have rather quiet days now. My brother is a soldier, my little sister is dead. With the child I had my fair share of trouble — yet I'd gladly take on all the trouble again, the child was so dear to me.
FAUST. An angel, if she was like you.

MARGARET. I raised her, and she loved me dearly. She was born after my father's death. My mother we gave up for lost, so wretched as she lay then; and she recovered very slowly, bit by bit. Then she could not even think of nursing the poor little worm herself, and so I raised her quite alone, with milk and water — so she became mine. On my arm, in my lap, she was friendly, kicked, grew up.
FAUST. You must have felt the purest happiness.

MARGARET. But surely many a hard hour too. The little one's cradle stood at night by my bed; she could hardly stir without my waking up. Sometimes I had to give her drink, sometimes lay her with me, sometimes, when she wouldn't be quiet, get up out of bed and walk her up and down in the chamber, dancing, and early in the day already at the washtub; then to the market and seeing to the hearth, and on and on, today like tomorrow. Things don't always go cheerfully, sir. But for that, the food tastes good, and rest tastes good.
[They walk past.]
MARTHA. The poor women are badly off: an old bachelor is hard to convert.
MEPHISTOPHELES. It would only depend on someone like you to teach me better.
MARTHA. Tell me straight out, sir — have you really found nothing yet? Has your heart not been bound somewhere?
MEPHISTOPHELES. The proverb says: One's own hearth, a good wife, are worth gold and pearls.
MARTHA. I mean, have you never had the inclination?
MEPHISTOPHELES. I have been received quite politely everywhere.
MARTHA. I meant to say — has it never become serious in your heart?
MEPHISTOPHELES. With women one should never dare to joke.
MARTHA. Ah, you don't understand me!
MEPHISTOPHELES. That truly grieves me! But I do understand — that you are very kind.
[They walk past.]
FAUST. Did you, little angel, recognize me again, just as I came into the garden?
MARGARET. Didn't you see? I cast my eyes down.
FAUST. And do you forgive the liberty I took? What my impudence ventured, when you came lately out of the cathedral.

MARGARET. I was bewildered; that had never happened to me. No one could say evil of me. Ah, I thought, did he see in your bearing something bold, something improper? It seemed to come over him at once, to deal straight with this girl. I confess it though! I didn't know what was beginning to stir in me on your behalf; but truly, I was quite cross with myself that I couldn't be more cross with you.
FAUST. Sweet darling!
MARGARET. Wait!
[She plucks a star-flower and pulls off the petals, one after the other.]
FAUST. What's this for? A bouquet?
MARGARET. No, just a game.
FAUST. How?
MARGARET. Go! You'll laugh at me.
[She picks and murmurs.]
FAUST. What are you murmuring?
MARGARET [half aloud]. He loves me — loves me not.
FAUST. You sweet face of heaven!
MARGARET [continues]. Loves me — not — Loves me — not —
[Picking off the last petal, with sweet joy.]
He loves me!
FAUST. Yes, my child! Let this flower-word be a divine pronouncement to you. He loves you! Do you understand what that means? He loves you!
[He grasps both her hands.]
MARGARET. I'm trembling!

FAUST. Oh, don't shudder! Let this look, let this pressure of the hand, tell you what is unspeakable: to give oneself wholly, and to feel a rapture that must be eternal! Eternal! — Its end would be despair. No, no end! No end!
MARGARET
[presses his hands, breaks free, and runs away. He stands a moment in thought, then follows her.]
MARTHA [coming up]. Night is falling.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Yes, and we'd better be off.

MARTHA. I'd ask you to stay longer, but it's too gossipy a place. It's as if no one had anything to do or work at, but to gape at every step and footfall of the neighbor. And one gets talked about, however one carries oneself. And our little couple?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Has flown off down that walk. Wanton summer-birds!
MARTHA. He seems fond of her.
MEPHISTOPHELES. And she of him too. That's the way of the world.

chapters.title: Garden Pavilion
paragraphs: MARGARET. Ah, you rascal, are you teasing me? I'll catch you!
[He kisses her.]
MARGARET [grasping him and returning the kiss].
Best of men! With all my heart I love you!
[MEPHISTOPHELES knocks. FAUST stamping.]
Who's there?
MEPHISTOPHELES. A good friend!
FAUST. A beast!
MEPHISTOPHELES. It is time, surely, to part.
MARTHA [coming up]. Yes, it's late, sir.
FAUST. May I not see you home?
MARGARET. My mother would — Farewell!
FAUST. Must I go then? Farewell!
MARTHA. Farewell!
MARGARET. Until we meet again, soon!
[Exit FAUST and MEPHISTOPHELES.]
MARGARET. Dear God! What such a man can think — every single thing! Ashamed, I just stand before him and say yes to everything. I'm a poor ignorant child — I don't understand what he sees in me.
[Exit.]

chapters.title: Forest and Cavern
paragraphs: FAUST. Sublime Spirit, you gave me, gave me everything for which I asked. Not in vain did you turn your face to me in the fire. You gave me magnificent nature for a kingdom, and the power to feel and enjoy her. You permit not just the cold, astonished visit, but allow me to look into her deep breast as into the heart of a friend. You lead the procession of the living past me and teach me to know my brothers in the silent thicket, in the air, and in the water. And when the storm rages and crashes through the forest, when the giant pine, falling, sweeps down the neighbor branches and neighbor trunks, crushing them, and the hill thunders dull and hollow at its fall — then you lead me to the safe cavern, show me to myself, and the secret deep wonders of my own breast open up. And when the pure moon climbs up before my gaze, soothing, then the silvery shapes of the prehistoric world hover up to me from rocky walls and from the moist thicket, and soften the strict pleasure of contemplation.

Oh, that nothing perfect is granted to man, I now feel. To this rapture which brings me near and nearer to the gods, you gave me the companion whom I can no longer do without — even though, cold and brazen, he degrades me before myself, and turns your gifts to nothing with a breath of words. He fans busily in my breast a wild fire for that beautiful image. So I reel from desire to enjoyment, and in enjoyment I languish for desire.
[Enter MEPHISTOPHELES.] MEPHISTOPHELES.
Have you led this kind of life long enough yet? How can it please you in the long run? It's well enough to try it once, then on to something new!
FAUST. I wish you had more to do than to plague me on a fair day.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Now, now! I gladly let you rest — you needn't say it to me in earnest. With a companion as ungracious, gruff, and crazy as you, there is truly little to lose. The whole day one has one's hands full! What pleases the gentleman and what one ought to leave alone, one can never tell from the gentleman's nose.
FAUST. That's just exactly the right tone! He wants thanks for boring me!

MEPHISTOPHELES. How would you, poor son of earth, have led your life without me? I cured you for a long time, after all, of the higgledy-piggledy of the imagination; and were it not for me, you'd already have walked off this terrestrial ball. Why are you sitting here in caves and rocky crevices like an owl? Why slurp nourishment, like a toad, out of dank moss and dripping stone? A fine, sweet pastime! The doctor still sticks fast in your body.
FAUST. Do you understand what new vital strength this wandering in the wilderness creates for me? Yes, if you could divine it, you'd be devil enough not to grudge me my happiness.

MEPHISTOPHELES. A supernatural pleasure! Lying out in night and dew on mountains, embracing earth and heaven rapturously, swelling oneself up into a divinity, burrowing through the marrow of earth with prophetic urge, feeling all six days' work in your bosom, enjoying I-don't-know-what in proud strength, soon flowing love-rapturously over into everything, the son of earth quite vanished, and then the lofty intuition —
[With a gesture.]
I dare not say how — to conclude. FAUST.
Shame on you!

MEPHISTOPHELES. That doesn't suit you. You have the right, well-mannered, to say "shame." One mustn't name before chaste ears what chaste hearts cannot do without. And in short, I grant you the pleasure of lying to yourself now and then; but you can't keep it up for long. You're already driven off again, and, if it lasts longer, worn down into madness or fear and horror. Enough of that! Your sweetheart sits indoors, and everything seems to her cramped and gloomy. You don't get out of her mind at all; she loves you overpoweringly. First your love-frenzy came pouring over, like a brook overflowing from melted snow. You poured it into her heart; now your brook is shallow again. I think, instead of throning in the woods, the great gentleman would do well to reward the poor monkey-young blood for her love. Time runs miserably long for her; she stands at the window, watches the clouds drift over the old city wall. "If I were a little bird!" — so runs her song day-long, half nights long. Sometimes she's lively, mostly grieved, sometimes thoroughly cried out, then again at peace, it seems — and always in love.
FAUST. Snake! Snake!
MEPHISTOPHELES [aside]. Yes! that I may catch you!
FAUST. Wretch! Be off from here, and don't name the lovely woman! Don't again bring the desire for her sweet body before my half-mad senses!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Then what's it for? She thinks you've fled — and half and half, you have.
FAUST. I'm near her — and were I ever so far, I can never forget her, never lose her. Yes, I already envy the body of the Lord, when her lips touch it.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Quite so, my friend! I've often envied you the twin pair that grazes among roses.
FAUST. Be off, you procurer!

MEPHISTOPHELES. Fine! You curse me, and I have to laugh. The God who created lad and girl recognized at once the noblest calling — to make opportunity too. Just be off — it's a great pity! You're supposed to go into your sweetheart's chamber, not to your death.

FAUST. What is the joy of heaven in her arms? Let me warm myself at her breast! Don't I always feel her need? Am I not the fugitive, the homeless one? The inhuman one without aim or rest, who, like a waterfall, raged from cliff to cliff, eagerly raging toward the abyss? And aside, in the small Alpine field, in the little hut, she with childlike dim senses, and all her household labors enclosed in that little world. And I, the God-hated, was not satisfied to seize the rocks and smash them to ruins! I had to undermine her, her peace! You, hell, had to have this victim! Help, Devil, to shorten the time of dread for me. What must happen, let it happen at once! May her fate crash down on me, and may she perish with me!

MEPHISTOPHELES. How it boils up again, glows again! Go in and console her, you fool! Where a little head like yours sees no exit, it imagines the end at once. Long live whoever bravely keeps his footing! You're otherwise pretty thoroughly bedeviled. I find nothing on earth more tasteless than a devil who despairs.

chapters.title: Gretchen's Room
paragraphs: GRETCHEN [alone at the spinning wheel].
My peace is gone, my heart is heavy. I shall find it never, and nevermore.
Where I do not have him is the grave to me; the whole world is poisoned for me.
My poor head is gone wild on me, my poor mind is torn to pieces.
My peace is gone, my heart is heavy. I shall find it never, and nevermore.
I look out the window only for him, I leave the house only for him.
His tall walk, his noble figure, the smile of his mouth, the power of his eyes,
and the magic flow of his speech, the press of his hand, and ah — his kiss!
My peace is gone, my heart is heavy. I shall find it never, and nevermore.
My breast longs for him. Ah, that I might grasp him and hold him! And kiss him as I wished, even if I should perish in his kisses!

chapters.title: Martha's Garden
paragraphs: FAUST. Whatever I can!
MARGARET. Now tell me, how do you stand with religion? You're a thoroughly good man, but I don't think you make much of it.
FAUST. Let it be, my child! You feel I'm fond of you; for those I love I would give body and blood. I want to rob no one of his feeling and his church.
MARGARET. That's not right — one must believe in it!
FAUST. Must one?
MARGARET. Ah! If only I could do something with you! You don't honor the holy sacraments either.
FAUST. I honor them.
MARGARET. But without longing. You haven't been to Mass, to confession, in a long time. Do you believe in God?
FAUST. My dearest, who dares say, "I believe in God"? You may ask priests or wise men, and their answer seems only mockery of the questioner.
MARGARET. So you don't believe?

FAUST. Don't misunderstand me, you sweet face! Who dares to name him? And who confess: I believe him? Who feel — and presume to say: I do not believe him? The All-embracer, the All-sustainer — does he not embrace and sustain you, me, himself? Does the heaven not vault itself overhead? Does the earth not lie firm down here? And don't eternal stars rise, looking on us friendly? Don't I look eye into eye with you, and doesn't everything press toward your head and heart, and weave in eternal mystery, invisible-visible, beside you? Fill your heart with this, as great as it is, and when in this feeling you are wholly blessed, then call it whatever you will — call it joy! heart! love! God! I have no name for it! Feeling is everything; the name is sound and smoke, clouding heaven's glow.
MARGARET. That is all very fine and good; the parson says about the same thing, only with a few different words.
FAUST. All hearts everywhere, under the heavenly day, say it — each in its own language. Why not I in mine?
MARGARET. To hear it like that, it might pass for tolerable; but yet things stand crooked all the same — for you have no Christianity.
FAUST. Dear child!
MARGARET. It has long pained me to see you in that company.
FAUST. How so?
MARGARET. The man you have with you is hateful to me in my deepest inward soul. In my whole life, nothing has so given me a stab to the heart as that man's repulsive face.
FAUST. Dear puppet, don't be afraid of him!

MARGARET. His presence sets my blood astir. Otherwise I'm well-disposed to all people; but as much as I long to see you, I have a secret horror of that man — and take him for a rogue besides! God forgive me if I do him wrong!
FAUST. Such oddities have to exist too.

MARGARET. I wouldn't want to live with the like of him! Whenever he comes through the door, he always looks so mocking, and half-enraged. One sees that he takes no part in anything; it's written on his forehead that he can love no soul. I feel so well in your arms, so free, so warmly given over — and his presence chokes me inwardly.
FAUST. You divining angel, you!

MARGARET. It overcomes me so much that, where he so much as approaches us, I even imagine I no longer love you. And when he is there, I could never pray, and that eats into my heart. — You, Heinrich, must feel the same.
FAUST. You simply have an antipathy!
MARGARET. I have to go now.
FAUST. Ah, can I never hang quietly a little hour at your breast, and press breast to breast and soul to soul?
MARGARET. Ah, if only I slept alone! Tonight I'd gladly leave the bolt open for you. But my mother does not sleep deeply, and if she caught us, I'd be dead on the spot!
FAUST. You angel, that's no trouble. Here is a little flask! Just three drops in her drink will gently veil nature in deep sleep.
MARGARET. What wouldn't I do for your sake? It surely won't harm her?
FAUST. Would I otherwise advise you to it, dearest?
MARGARET. When I look at you, dearest man, I don't know what drives me to your will — I have already done so much for you that there's almost nothing left for me to do.
[Exit.]
[Enter MEPHISTOPHELES.] MEPHISTOPHELES.
The little monkey-girl! Has she gone?
FAUST. Have you been spying again?

MEPHISTOPHELES. I overheard it all in detail. The doctor has been catechized! I hope it does you good. The girls are very interested in whether one is pious and plain in the old style. They think: if he ducks there, he'll follow us along too.

FAUST. You monster, you don't see how this faithful, dear soul, full of her belief — which is the only thing that gives her bliss — torments herself, holily, that she should consider her dearest man lost.
MEPHISTOPHELES. You supersensual, sensual suitor, a little maiden leads you by the nose.
FAUST. You misshapen offspring of muck and fire!

MEPHISTOPHELES. And she understands physiognomy masterfully. In my presence she feels — she doesn't know how. My little mask there divines a hidden sense; she feels that I am surely a genius, perhaps even the devil himself. Now tonight —?
FAUST. What's that to you?
MEPHISTOPHELES. I take my pleasure in it!

chapters.title: At the Well
paragraphs: LIESCHEN. Have you heard nothing of little Bärbel?
GRETCHEN. Not a word. I see very few people.
LIESCHEN. It's certain — Sibylle told me today! She's been led astray at last. So much for putting on airs!
GRETCHEN. How so?
LIESCHEN. It stinks of it! She's feeding two now when she eats and drinks.
GRETCHEN. Ah!

LIESCHEN. So she's gotten what she deserves at last. How long she clung to that fellow! There was such walking out, such leading to the village and the dance-floor — she had to be the first everywhere. He always courted her with pastry and wine; she fancied something of her beauty, but was so dishonorable that she wasn't ashamed to take presents from him. There was such cuddling and such smooching — and now the little flower is gone too!
GRETCHEN. The poor thing!

LIESCHEN. You feel sorry for her even now! When our sort was at the spinning, our mother kept us in at night — and there she stood sweetly with her lover, on the door-bench and in the dark passageway, where no hour was too long for them. So now she may bow down and do church-penance in the sinner's smock!
GRETCHEN. He'll surely take her for his wife.
LIESCHEN. He'd be a fool! A nimble lad has plenty of air to breathe elsewhere. And he's gone too.
GRETCHEN. That's not nice!
LIESCHEN. If she gets him, things will go badly for her. The boys will tear her bridal wreath, and we'll scatter chopped straw before her door!
[Exit.]
GRETCHEN [going home].

How harshly I used to scold, when I saw a poor girl go astray! How my tongue could not find words enough for the sins of others! How black it seemed to me — and however much I blackened it, it was never black enough — and I crossed myself and put on airs, and now I am bared to sin myself! Yet — everything that drove me to it, God! was so good — ah, was so dear!

chapters.title: Donjon
paragraphs: GRETCHEN [putting fresh flowers in the jars].
Ah, incline, you of many sorrows, your face mercifully toward my distress!
Sword in your heart, with a thousand pains, you gaze up to your Son's death.
You look up to the Father, and send sighs up for his and your distress.
Who feels how the pain digs in my bones? What my poor heart fears here, what it trembles for, what it longs for — you alone know, you alone!
Wherever I go, how it aches, how it aches, how it aches in my breast here! Ah, I am hardly alone before I weep, I weep, I weep — the heart breaks within me.
The flowerpots before my window I sprinkled with tears, alas, when I broke these flowers for you in the early morning.
When the sun shone bright into my chamber, early up, I was already sitting up in all my misery in my bed.
Help! Save me from shame and death! Ah, incline, you of many sorrows, your face mercifully toward my distress!

chapters.title: Night. Street before Gretchen's Door
paragraphs: FAUST. How, from the window there of the sacristy, the gleam of the eternal little lamp flickers upward and dimmer, dimmer wanes sideways, while darkness presses in all around! That's how it looks, nightly, in my breast.

MEPHISTOPHELES. And I feel like a slim little tomcat, slipping along the fire-ladder, then softly stroking past the walls. I feel quite virtuous about it — a bit of thief's lust, a bit of randiness. Through every limb the splendid Walpurgis Night is already haunting me. It comes again the day after tomorrow — then one knows why one is keeping watch.
FAUST. Is the treasure rising up meanwhile? The one I see shimmering down there.
MEPHISTOPHELES. You'll soon experience the joy of lifting the little kettle out. I peeked into it lately — there are splendid lion-dollars inside.
FAUST. Not a piece of jewelry? Not a ring? To deck my dear sweetheart with.
MEPHISTOPHELES. I did see something of the sort — a kind of pearl-strand.
FAUST. That's good! It pains me to go to her without a present.

MEPHISTOPHELES. It shouldn't even bother you to enjoy something for free as well. Now, while heaven glows full of stars, you shall hear a real piece of art: I'll sing her a moralizing song, to befool her more surely.
[Sings to a zither.]
What are you doing here, little Catherine, before your sweetheart's door at the early light of day? Let it, let it be! He'll let you in as a maiden, but as a maiden not let you out.
Take care! Once it's done, then good night, you poor, poor things! If you love yourselves, do nothing for any thief out of love — except with the ring on your finger.
[VALENTINE steps forward.] Whom are you luring here? By the elements! Cursed rat-catcher! To the devil first the instrument! And to the devil after it the singer!
MEPHISTOPHELES. The zither is broken! Nothing more to be done with that.
VALENTINE. Now it's going to come to skull-splitting!
MEPHISTOPHELES [to FAUST]. Doctor, don't give way! Quick! Stay close to me — let me lead you. Out with your feather-duster! Just thrust away! I'll parry.
VALENTINE. Parry that!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Why not?
VALENTINE. And that!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Certainly!
VALENTINE. I think the devil himself is fencing! What is this? Already my hand is going lame.
MEPHISTOPHELES [to FAUST]. Strike!
VALENTINE [falls]. O woe!

MEPHISTOPHELES. Now the lout is tame! But away! We must vanish at once: for already a murderous outcry is rising up. I know how to handle the police capitally — but the criminal court goes badly with me.
MARTHA [at the window]. Out! Out!
GRETCHEN [at the window]. Quick, a light here!
MARTHA [as before]. People are scolding and brawling, shouting and fighting.
PEOPLE. There lies one already dead!
MARTHA [stepping out]. Have the murderers fled, then?
GRETCHEN [stepping out]. Who lies here?
PEOPLE. Your mother's son.
GRETCHEN. Almighty God! What misery!
VALENTINE. I am dying! That's quickly said, and even more quickly done. Why do you stand there, women, weeping and lamenting? Come here and listen to me!
[All step around him.]
My Gretchen, see! You are still young, you are not yet shrewd enough; you handle your affairs badly. I'll tell you in confidence: you are now once and for all a whore — so let it just be so.
GRETCHEN. My brother! God! What does this mean?

VALENTINE. Leave our Lord God out of the joke. What's done is unfortunately done, and as it can go, so it will go. You began secretly with one — soon there'll be several, and once a dozen has had you, the whole town will too.

When shame is first born, it is brought into the world secretly, and one draws the veil of night over its head and ears; yes, one would gladly murder it. But if it grows and makes itself big, then it goes about openly even in daytime — and yet has not become any prettier. The uglier its face becomes, the more it seeks the light of day.

I truly already see the time when all decent burgher-folk will turn aside from you, you slut, as if from an infected corpse! Your heart shall fail you in your body when they look you in the eye! You shall wear no more golden chains! Stand no more at the altar in the church! Take no more pleasure at the dance in a fine lace collar! Hide yourself in some dark corner of misery among beggars and cripples — and even if God forgives you, on earth you shall be cursed!
MARTHA. Commend your soul to God's mercy! Will you load yourself yet with blasphemy?
VALENTINE. If only I could lay hands on your withered body, you shameful pimping woman! Then I'd hope to find rich measure of forgiveness for all my sins.
GRETCHEN. My brother! What hellish torment!
VALENTINE. I tell you, leave the tears alone! When you parted with your honor, you gave me the heaviest stab to the heart. I go through death-sleep to God as a soldier and a man of honor.
[Dies.]

chapters.title: Cathedral
paragraphs: EVIL SPIRIT. How different it was for you, Gretchen, when you, still full of innocence, stepped here to the altar, stammering prayers from your worn little prayer-book, half child's-play, half God in your heart — Gretchen! Where is your head? In your heart, what crime? Are you praying for your mother's soul, that, through you, slept over into long, long torment? On your threshold — whose blood? — And under your heart, doesn't something already stir, swelling, frightening you and itself with its prophetic presence?
GRETCHEN. Woe! Woe! If only I were free of the thoughts that go to and fro within me, against me!
CHORUS. Dies irae, dies illa, solvet saeclum in favilla. [Day of wrath, that day shall dissolve the world in ashes.]
[Sound of organ.]
EVIL SPIRIT. Wrath seizes you! The trumpet sounds! The graves tremble! And your heart, raised again from ashen rest to flames of torment, leaps up!
GRETCHEN. Were I out of here! It is as if the organ stopped my breath, the singing dissolved my heart at the deepest place.
CHORUS. Judex ergo cum sedebit, quidquid latet adparebit, nil inultum remanebit. [When therefore the judge takes his seat, whatever is hidden will appear; nothing will remain unavenged.]
GRETCHEN. It grows so cramped here! The wall-pillars hold me fast! The vault presses me down! — Air!
EVIL SPIRIT. Hide yourself! Sin and shame stay not hidden. Air? Light? Woe to you!
CHORUS. Quid sum miser tunc dicturus? Quem patronum rogaturus? Cum vix justus sit securus. [What shall I, wretch, then say? What patron shall I beg, when scarcely the just man is secure?]
EVIL SPIRIT. The transfigured ones turn their faces away from you. The pure shudder to reach out their hands to you. Woe!
CHORUS. Quid sum miser tunc dicturus? [What shall I, wretch, then say?]
GRETCHEN. Neighbor! Your smelling-bottle! —
[She falls in a faint.]

chapters.title: Walpurgis Night
paragraphs: MEPHISTOPHELES. Don't you long for a broomstick? I myself wish I had the toughest billy-goat. On this path we're still far from the goal.

FAUST. As long as I still feel fresh on my legs, this knotted stick is enough for me. What good is it to shorten the road? — To creep along through the labyrinth of valleys, then to climb up these cliffs from which the spring eternally springs gushing — that's the joy that seasons such paths! Spring is already weaving in the birches, and even the fir already feels it. Shouldn't it work on our limbs too?

MEPHISTOPHELES. Truly I feel nothing of it! It's wintry in my body. I'd wish for snow and frost on my course. How sadly the imperfect disk of the red moon climbs up with its late glow! And shines so badly that at every step one runs into a tree, into a rock! Allow me to ask a will-o'-the-wisp! There I see one, just merrily burning. Hey there, my friend! May I summon you to us? Why blaze so vainly? Be so good as to light us up there!
WILL-O'-THE-WISP. Out of reverence, I hope, I shall succeed in compelling my light nature; usually our course goes only zigzag.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Ay, ay! It's thinking of imitating men. Just go straight, in the devil's name! Or I'll blow out your flickering life.

WILL-O'-THE-WISP. I see clearly you're the master of the house, and I'll gladly accommodate myself to you. But consider! The mountain is bewitched today, and if a will-o'-the-wisp is to show you the way, you mustn't take it too exactly.

FAUST, MEPHISTOPHELES, WILL-O'-THE-WISP [in alternating song]. Into the realms of dream and magic we have, it seems, entered. Lead us well and earn yourself credit, that we may soon press forward into the wide, desolate spaces.
See trees behind trees, how they shift quickly past, and the cliffs that bow down, and the long rocky noses, how they snore, how they blow!

Through the stones, through the grass, brook and streamlet hurry down. Do I hear murmuring? Do I hear songs? Do I hear sweet love-laments, voices of those days of heaven? What we hope, what we love! And the echo, like the legend of old times, rings back.

Tu-whoo! Tu-whoo! sounds nearer; owl and lapwing and jay — have they all stayed awake? Are those salamanders through the bushes? Long legs, fat bellies. And the roots like snakes wind out of rock and sand; stretching strange bands to terrify us, to catch us; out of living, coarse knots they stretch out polyp-fibers toward the wanderer. And the mice — thousand-colored, in droves, through the moss and through the heath! And the fireflies fly in dense swarming trains as a confusing escort.
But tell me — are we standing still? Or going on? Everything, everything seems to whirl: rock and trees, the faces grimacing, and the wandering lights that multiply and bloat themselves up.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Bravely seize my coat-tail! Here's a kind of mid-summit, where with astonishment one sees how Mammon glows in the mountain.

FAUST. How strangely a dim red dawn-glow gleams through the depths! And it scents its way even down into the deepest gulfs of the abyss. There a vapor rises, here clouds drift; here a glow shines through mist and veil, then it creeps like a delicate thread, then breaks forth like a spring. Here it winds a whole stretch with a hundred veins through the valley, and here in the close corner it isolates itself all at once. There sparks spray nearby, like scattered golden sand. But look! The whole height of the rock-wall ignites itself.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Doesn't Lord Mammon splendidly light up the palace for this festival? It's lucky you've seen it; I already sense the impetuous guests.
FAUST. How the wind-bride rages through the air! With what blows she strikes my neck!

MEPHISTOPHELES. You must seize the rock's old ribs, or she'll throw you down into this gulf's grave. A mist thickens the night. Hear how it crashes through the woods! The owls fly up, frightened. Hear the pillars splintering of evergreen palaces. The cooing and breaking of the boughs, the mighty roar of the trunks! The roots' creaking and yawning! In a fearfully tangled fall, they all crash down upon one another, and through the smashed-up clefts the winds hiss and howl. Do you hear voices in the heights? In the distance, in the near? Yes, all along the mountain a furious magic-song is streaming.

WITCHES IN CHORUS. The witches are heading to the Brocken; the stubble is yellow, the seedling green. There the great mob gathers, Lord Urian sits up on top. So it goes over stone and stick — the witch farts, the goat stinks.
VOICE. Old Baubo comes alone — she rides on a sow.
CHORUS. So honor to whom honor is due! Lady Baubo to the front, and lead the way! A worthy sow with mother on top — the whole witch-mob follows behind.
VOICE. Which way did you come?
VOICE. Over the Ilsenstein! There I peered into the owl's nest. She made a pair of eyes!
VOICE. Oh, ride to hell! Why ride so fast?
VOICE. She's flayed me — just look at the wounds!
WITCHES' CHORUS. The way is broad, the way is long. What kind of crazy press is this? The fork pricks, the broom scratches; the child suffocates, the mother bursts.
WIZARDS [Half Chorus].
We creep like the snail in his house; the women are all up ahead. For when going to the Evil One's house, woman has a thousand steps' lead.
OTHER HALF. We don't take it that strictly. With a thousand steps the woman does it, but however she may hurry, with one leap the man does it.
VOICE FROM ABOVE. Come along, come along, from the rocky lake!
VOICES FROM BELOW. We'd gladly come up to the heights. We wash, and we are entirely shining clean — but eternally barren too.
BOTH CHORUSES. The wind falls silent, the star flees, the dim moon gladly hides itself. In its rushing, the magic chorus sprays many thousands of fire-sparks forth.
VOICE FROM BELOW. Stop! Stop!
VOICE FROM ABOVE. Who's calling there from the rocky cleft?
VOICE BELOW. Take me with you! Take me with you! I've been climbing three hundred years and can't reach the summit. I'd love to be with my own kind.
BOTH CHORUSES. The broom carries, the stick carries, the fork carries, the goat carries. Whoever cannot lift himself today is a forever-lost man.
HALF-WITCH BELOW. I trip along, after such a long time — how far ahead the others are already! I have no peace at home, and don't get there here either.
CHORUS OF WITCHES. The salve gives the witches courage, a rag is good for a sail, every trough is a good ship; he who hasn't flown today never flies.
BOTH CHORUSES. And when we draw round the summit, then sweep along the ground, and cover the heath far and wide with your swarm of witchhood.
[They settle down.]

MEPHISTOPHELES. How they crowd and shove, rustle and clatter! How they hiss and stir, pull and prattle! How they shine, spray, stink, and burn! A real witch-element! Just hold tight to me! or we'll soon be parted. Where are you?
FAUST [in the distance]. Here!

MEPHISTOPHELES. What! Already swept off there? Then I'll have to use householder's right. Make way! Squire Voland is coming. Make way, sweet rabble, make way! Here, Doctor, take hold of me! And now, in one leap, let's get out of the press; it's too crazy, even for my kind. Something's shining over there with quite a peculiar gleam — something draws me to those bushes. Come, come! we'll slip in there.
FAUST. You spirit of contradiction! Lead on, then. I think it was wisely planned: we wander to the Brocken on Walpurgis Night, only to isolate ourselves here as we please.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Just look — what colorful flames! It's a lively club gathered together. In a smaller party one is not alone.
FAUST. But I'd rather be up above! Already I see glow and whirling smoke. There the crowd streams to the Evil One; there many a riddle must be solved.

MEPHISTOPHELES. But many a riddle is also tied. Just let the great world bustle on; we'll set up house here in quiet. It's an old custom, after all, that within the great world one makes little worlds. There I see young witches naked and bare, and old ones who shrewdly veil themselves. Be friendly, just for my sake — the trouble is small, the fun is great. I hear something sounding from instruments! Damned scraping! One has to get used to it. Come on! Come on! It can't be otherwise — I'll step up and bring you in, and bind you again to me anew. What do you say, friend? It's no small space. Just look there! You can hardly see the end. A hundred fires burn in a row; people dance, chatter, cook, drink, make love. Now tell me, where can you find anything better?
FAUST. Will you, in introducing us here, present yourself as wizard or as devil?

MEPHISTOPHELES. True, I'm very used to going incognito; but on a gala day one shows one's order. A garter doesn't distinguish me, but the horse's foot is honored at home here. Do you see that snail there? She comes crawling along; with her groping face, she's already smelled out something about me. Even if I wished, I couldn't deny myself here. Just come! From fire to fire we'll go; I am the matchmaker, you are the suitor.
[To some sitting around dying coals.]
You old gentlemen, what are you doing here at the edge? I'd praise you if I found you nicely in the middle, surrounded by revelry and the rush of youth. Each is alone enough at home.
GENERAL. Who would trust nations? However much one has done for them — for in a people, as with women, youth always stands at the top.
MINISTER. Now things are far too removed from the right. I praise me the good old days; for then, when we counted for everything, that was the right golden age.
PARVENU. Truly we weren't fools either, and often did what we shouldn't have. But now everything is turning upside down, just when we wanted to hold it firm.
AUTHOR. Who would even read a writing now of moderately clever content! And as for the dear young folk — they have never been so impudent.
MEPHISTOPHELES [suddenly appearing very old].
I feel the people ripe for the Day of Judgment, since I'm climbing the witch-mountain for the last time, and because my little cask runs muddy — so the world too is on its last legs.

OLD-CLOTHES WITCH. Gentlemen, don't pass by like that! Don't let the chance slip! Look attentively at my wares — many things are here. And yet there's nothing in my shop that doesn't have its like on earth, that hasn't at some time done some serious harm to mankind and the world. There's no dagger here from which blood hasn't flowed; no chalice from which devouring hot poison hasn't been poured into a perfectly healthy body; no jewel that hasn't seduced a lovable woman; no sword that hasn't broken a bond, hasn't perhaps stabbed an opponent in the back.
MEPHISTOPHELES. Cousin! She doesn't understand the times. Done is done! Done is done! Stick to novelties — only novelties draw us in.
FAUST. May I just not forget myself! I call this a real fair!
MEPHISTOPHELES. The whole whirl strives upward; you think you're pushing and you're being pushed.
FAUST. Who is that, then?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Look at her closely! That is Lilith.
FAUST. Who?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Adam's first wife. Beware of her beautiful hair, of this finery with which alone she shines. When with this she catches the young man, she does not soon let him go again.
FAUST. There sit two — the old one with the young; they've already had a good leap!
MEPHISTOPHELES. Today there's no rest. A new dance is starting; come on, we'll join in.
FAUST [dancing with the young one]. Once I had a beautiful dream; I saw an apple tree, two beautiful apples gleamed on it. They tempted me, I climbed up.
THE BEAUTIFUL ONE. You greatly desire the little apples, ever since Paradise. With joy I feel myself moved that my garden too bears such things.
