MEPHISTOPHELES [with the old one]. Once I had a wild dream; I saw a split tree that had a vast hole — vast as it was, it pleased me well.
THE OLD ONE. I offer my best greeting to the knight with the horse's foot! Let him keep a proper plug ready, if he doesn't shy from the great hole.
BROCKTOPHANTASMIST. Cursed folk! What do you presume to do? Hasn't it been long proven to you? A spirit never stands on proper feet; now you actually dance, just like us other humans!
THE BEAUTIFUL ONE [dancing]. What does that one want at our ball?

FAUST [dancing]. Eh! He's everywhere. He has to judge what others dance. If he can't carp at every step, then the step is as good as not taken. He's most annoyed as soon as we go forward. If you'd just turn around in a circle, the way he does it in his old mill, he would still pass it as good — especially if you'd salute him for it.

BROCKTOPHANTASMIST. You're still here! No, this is unheard-of! Just disappear! We've enlightened things, after all. Devil-trash asks no rules. We are so clever, and yet there are still ghosts in Tegel. How long have I been sweeping out the delusion, and never does it get clean — that is unheard-of!
THE BEAUTIFUL ONE. Then stop boring us here!
BROCKTOPHANTASMIST. I'll say it to your faces, you spirits — I won't tolerate the despotism of the spirit. My spirit can't exercise it.
[The dance continues.]
Today, I see, nothing's going to succeed for me. But I take a journey along all the same, and still hope, before my last step, to subdue the devils and the poets.
MEPHISTOPHELES. He'll soon sit himself down in a puddle. That's how he relieves himself, and when leeches feast on his rump, he is cured of spirits and of intellect.
[To FAUST, who has stepped out of the dance.]
Why have you let the lovely girl go? She sang to you so sweetly for the dance.
FAUST. Ah, in the middle of singing, a red mouse jumped out of her mouth.
MEPHISTOPHELES. That's something fine! One doesn't take it strictly. At least the mouse wasn't gray. Who asks about such things in a shepherd's hour?
FAUST. Then I saw —
MEPHISTOPHELES. What?

FAUST. Mephisto, do you see, over there, a pale, lovely child, alone and far off? She drags slowly from the spot — she seems to walk with closed feet. I must confess, it seems to me, that she resembles dear Gretchen.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Just leave it alone! No good comes to anyone from that. It's a magic-image, lifeless, an idol. To meet it is not good; the rigid gaze freezes the human blood, and one is almost turned to stone — you've heard of Medusa.
FAUST. Truly they are a dead one's eyes, that no loving hand closed. That is the breast that Gretchen offered me, that is the sweet body I enjoyed.
MEPHISTOPHELES. That is the witchcraft, you easily seduced fool! For to everyone she appears as his own sweetheart.
FAUST. What rapture! What pain! I cannot tear myself from this gaze. How strangely a single red cord adorns this lovely neck — no broader than the back of a knife!

MEPHISTOPHELES. Quite right! I see it as well. She can also carry her head under her arm, since Perseus chopped it off for her. — Always this taste for delusion! Come on up to the little hill; here it's as merry as in the Prater. And, unless I've been bewitched, I really do see a theater. What's playing?

SERVIBILIS. They're starting again at once. A new piece — the last piece of seven, as is the custom here. A dilettante wrote it, and dilettantes will play it too. Forgive me, gentlemen, if I disappear; I get the dilettante's itch to raise the curtain.
MEPHISTOPHELES. If I find you on the Blocksberg, I find that good — for there you belong.

chapters.title: Walpurgis Night's Dream
paragraphs: STAGE-MANAGER. Today, for once, we'll rest, brave sons of Mieding. Old mountain and damp valley — that's the whole scene!
HERALD. For the wedding to be golden, fifty years must have passed. But once the strife is over, the gold-en is dearer to me.
OBERON. Spirits, if you are where I am, show it in these hours. King and Queen, they are again united.
PUCK. Here comes Puck, and turns crosswise, and trails his foot in the round. A hundred come behind him to rejoice with him.
ARIEL. Ariel sets the song astir in tones heavenly pure. His sound lures many grimaces, but it lures the lovely too.
OBERON. Husbands and wives who would get along — learn it from the two of us! When two are to love each other, you only have to part them.
TITANIA. If the husband sulks and the wife frets — just take her smartly, lead her to the south for me, and him to the north's far end.
ORCHESTRA TUTTI
[Fortissimo.]
Fly-snout and mosquito-nose, with all their kin, frog in the foliage and cricket in the grass — those are the musicians!
SOLO. See, here comes the bagpipe! It's the soap-bubble. Hear the hicketty-snickerty-snack through its blunt nose.
SPIRIT JUST FORMING. Spider-foot and toad-belly, and tiny wings for the little wretch! True, no little animal will result, but a little poem certainly will.
A YOUNG COUPLE. Small step and high leap through honey-dew and fragrances. True, you trip along enough for me — but it doesn't go up into the air.
CURIOUS TRAVELER. Isn't this masquerade-mockery? Should I trust my eyes? To see Oberon, the lovely god, here today as well!
ORTHODOX. No claws, no tail! Yet it remains beyond doubt: just like the gods of Greece, he too is a devil.
NORTHERN ARTIST. What I take in today is truly only sketches; but in good time I'll prepare myself for the Italian journey.
PURIST. Ah! My misfortune brings me here. How they carouse! And of the whole witch-host, only two are powdered.
YOUNG WITCH. Powder is, like a skirt, for old and gray little wives, so I sit naked on my goat and show off a sturdy little body.
MATRON. We have too much breeding to spar with you here; but I do hope you'll rot away, just as you are, young and tender.
BANDMASTER. Fly-snout and mosquito-nose, don't swarm around me at the naked one! Frog in the foliage and cricket in the grass — keep at least to the beat!
WEATHERVANE
[turning to one side.]
Society as one could wish for. Truly nothing but brides! And bachelors, man for man, the most hopeful people.
WEATHERVANE
[turning to the other side.]
And if the ground does not open up to swallow them all, then I'll spring with nimble run straight into hell.
XENIEN. As insects we are here, with little sharp scissors, to honor Satan, our Lord Father, as is fitting.
HENNINGS. Look! How they jest naïvely all together in their close throng. In the end, they'll even claim that they have good hearts.
MUSAGETES. I'd gladly lose myself in this witch-host, for sooner could I lead these than the Muses.
FORMER GENIUS OF THE AGE.
With the right people you can become something. Come, take hold of my coat-tail! The Blocksberg, like the German Parnassus, has after all a very broad summit.
CURIOUS TRAVELER. Tell me, what's that stiff fellow's name? He walks with proud strides. He sniffs out whatever he can sniff out. "He's tracking Jesuits."
CRANE. I like to fish in clear water and in muddy too; that's why you see the pious gentleman mingling with devils too.
WORLDLY ONE. Yes, for the pious, believe me, everything is a vehicle. Here on the Blocksberg they form many a little conventicle.
DANCER. Here comes a new chorus, perhaps? I hear distant drums. Don't be disturbed! In the reeds it's the unison bitterns.
DOGMATIST. I won't be shouted off course, neither by criticism nor by doubt. The devil must be something, after all — otherwise how would there be any devils?
IDEALIST. Imagination in my mind is this time too domineering. Truly, if I am all this, then I am crazy today.
REALIST. Existence is a real torment to me, and must annoy me thoroughly; for the first time I do not stand here firm on my feet.
SUPERNATURALIST. With great pleasure I'm here, and rejoice with these; for from devils I can, after all, infer good spirits.
SKEPTIC. They follow the trail of the little flames and believe they're near the treasure. Doubt only rhymes with devil — there I'm right at home.
BANDMASTER. Frog in the foliage and cricket in the grass, cursed dilettantes! Fly-snout and mosquito-nose — you are at least musicians!
THE NIMBLE ONES. Sans-souci, that's the name of the troop of merry creatures. On our feet it no longer goes — so we walk on our heads.
THE CLUMSY ONES. Earlier we cadged many a tidbit, but now — God commend us! Our shoes are danced through; we run on naked soles.
WILL-O'-THE-WISPS. From the swamp we come, where we first sprang up; though already in the round dance here, the gleaming gallants.
SHOOTING STAR. From the heights I shot down here in the gleam of star and fire; I lie now crosswise in the grass — who'll help me to my feet?
THE MASSIVE ONES. Make way, make way, and all around! So the little grasses go down. Spirits come, and spirits — they too have clumsy limbs.
PUCK. Don't tread so heavily, like baby elephants. And the heaviest tread of this day shall be Puck, sturdy himself.
ARIEL. If loving Nature, if the spirit, gave you wings, then follow my light trail up to the rose-hill!
ORCHESTRA [pianissimo].
Cloud-train and mist-veil clear themselves from above. Air in the leaves and wind in the reed — and everything is scattered.

chapters.title: Gloomy Day. Field
paragraphs: FAUST. In misery! Despairing! Wretchedly wandering long upon the earth and now imprisoned! As a criminal, locked up in the dungeon for terrible torments — that lovely, unhappy creature! To this point — to this! — Treacherous, worthless spirit, and you have kept this from me! — Just stand, stand there! Roll your devilish eyes ragingly in your head! Stand and defy me with your unbearable presence! Captured! In irretrievable misery! Handed over to evil spirits and to a judging, feelingless humanity! And meanwhile you cradled me in tasteless distractions, hid her growing anguish from me, and let her perish helpless!
MEPHISTOPHELES. She is not the first.

FAUST. Dog! Abominable beast! — Change him, you infinite Spirit! Change the worm back into his dog-shape, in which he often, by night, took pleasure in trotting before me, rolling under the harmless wanderer's feet, and hanging on the shoulders of the man stumbling down. Change him back into his favorite form, so that he may crawl on his belly in the sand before me, and I may trample him with my feet, the outcast! — Not the first! — Anguish! Anguish! incomprehensible to any human soul, that more than one creature should sink into the depth of this misery — that the first was not enough to atone for the guilt of all the rest in its writhing death-agony before the eyes of the eternally Forgiving! It tears my marrow and life through the misery of this one — you grin coldly over the fate of thousands.

MEPHISTOPHELES. Now we're at the border of our wits again, where you humans go off your heads. Why do you make common cause with us, if you can't see it through? You want to fly, and yet you aren't safe from dizziness? Did we force ourselves on you, or you on us?

FAUST. Don't bare your greedy teeth at me like that! It disgusts me! — Great, magnificent Spirit, who deigned to appear to me, who knows my heart and my soul, why chain me to that shameful companion, who feeds on harm and gloats on ruin?
MEPHISTOPHELES. Are you finished?
FAUST. Save her! Or woe to you! The most ghastly curse on you for thousands of years!
MEPHISTOPHELES. I cannot loose the bonds of the Avenger, nor open his bolts. — Save her! — Who was it that plunged her into ruin? I or you?
FAUST [looking wildly around]. MEPHISTOPHELES.

Are you reaching for the thunder? Just as well that it was not given to you wretched mortals! To smash the innocent who answers you back — that is just like a tyrant venting himself in his embarrassments.
FAUST. Bring me there! She must be free!

MEPHISTOPHELES. And the danger you expose yourself to? Know that on the city still lies blood-guilt from your hand. Over the place of the slain man, avenging spirits hover and lie in wait for the murderer's return.
FAUST. Even that from you? Murder and death of a world upon you, monster! Lead me there, I say, and free her!

MEPHISTOPHELES. I'll lead you, and what I can do, listen! Have I all power in heaven and on earth? I'll cloud the warder's senses; you take the keys and lead her out by human hand. I'll keep watch! The magic horses are ready; I'll carry you off. That much I can do!
FAUST. Up and away!

chapters.title: Night. Open Field
paragraphs: MEPHISTOPHELES. I don't know what they're cooking and brewing. FAUST.
Soaring up, soaring down, bowing, bending. MEPHISTOPHELES.
A witches' guild. FAUST.
They scatter and consecrate. MEPHISTOPHELES.
Past! Past!

chapters.title: Dungeon
paragraphs: [FAUST, with a bunch of keys and a lamp, before a small iron door.]

FAUST. A long-disused shudder seizes me; the whole anguish of mankind takes hold of me. Here she dwells behind this damp wall, and her crime was a sweet delusion! You hesitate to go to her! You fear to see her again! On! Your wavering brings death nearer.
[He grasps the lock. From within someone is singing.]
GRETCHEN. My mother, the whore, who killed me! My father, the rogue, who ate me! My little sister gathered up the bones in a cool place; there I became a pretty wood-bird. Fly away, fly away!
FAUST [unlocking]. She does not suspect that her lover is listening, hears the chains rattle, the straw rustle.
[He enters.]
MARGARET [hiding herself on her pallet]. Woe! Woe! They are coming. Bitter death!
FAUST [softly]. Quiet! Quiet! I'm coming to free you.
MARGARET [rolling herself before him]. If you are a human, then feel my distress.
FAUST. You will rouse the guards from sleep with your shouting!
[He grasps the chains to unlock them.]
MARGARET [on her knees]. Who, executioner, has given you this power over me? You're already taking me at midnight! Have mercy and let me live! Isn't tomorrow morning early enough?
[She stands up.]

I'm still so young, so young! And am I to die already! I was beautiful too, and that was my ruin. The lover was near; now he is far. The wreath lies torn, the flowers scattered. Don't grasp me so violently! Spare me! What have I done to you? Don't let me beg in vain — I've never set eyes on you in my life!
FAUST. Will I survive this anguish!

MARGARET. I am wholly in your power now. Just let me first nurse the child. I cradled it the whole night; they took it from me to grieve me, and now they say I have killed it. And never will I be glad again. They sing songs about me! It is wicked of the people! An old fairy tale ends like that — who told them to apply it to me?
FAUST [throwing himself down]. A lover lies at your feet to unlock the bondage of your misery.
MARGARET [throwing herself down to him]. O let us kneel and call upon the saints! See — under these steps, under the threshold, hell is seething! The Evil One, with terrible rage, makes a roar!
FAUST [aloud]. Gretchen! Gretchen!
MARGARET [listening attentively]. That was the lover's voice!
[She springs up. The chains fall away.]

Where is he? I've heard him calling. I am free! No one shall hold me back. To his neck I'll fly, on his bosom I'll lie! He called "Gretchen!" He stood on the threshold. Through the howling and clattering of hell, through the savage, devilish mockery, I knew the sweet, the loving tone.
FAUST. It's me!
MARGARET. It's you! Oh, say it once more!
[Grasping him.]

It's him! It's him! Where is all the torment gone? Where the dread of the dungeon, the chains? It's you! You've come to save me. I am saved! — Already the street is back, where I first saw you. And the cheerful garden where Martha and I are waiting for you.
FAUST [striving to go].
Come with me! Come with me!
MARGARET. O wait! I'd so gladly stay where you stay.
[Caressing him.]
FAUST. Hurry! If you don't hurry, we shall pay for it dearly.

MARGARET. What? You can no longer kiss? My friend, so short a time away from me, and you've forgotten how to kiss? Why am I so anxious at your neck — when otherwise from your words, your glances, a whole heaven would press in on me, and you kissed me as if you would smother me. Kiss me! Or I will kiss you!
[She embraces him.]
Oh woe! Your lips are cold, are mute. Where has your loving gone? Who took it from me?
[She turns away from him.]
FAUST. Come! Follow me! Sweetheart, take courage! I'll embrace you with thousandfold ardor — only follow me! That's all I ask of you!
MARGARET [turning to him]. And is it really you? And is it certainly you?
FAUST. It's me! Come with me!
MARGARET. You loosen the fetters, you take me again into your lap. How is it that you don't shrink from me? — And do you know, my friend, whom you are freeing?
FAUST. Come! Come! The deep night is already giving way.

MARGARET. I have killed my mother, I have drowned my child. Wasn't it given to you and me? To you too — It's you! I can hardly believe it. Give me your hand! It's no dream! Your dear hand! — But oh, it's wet! Wipe it off! There seems to be — blood on it. Oh God! What have you done! Sheathe the sword, I beg you!
FAUST. Let what is past be past. You're killing me.

MARGARET. No, you must remain alive! I'll describe the graves to you, which you must take care of right tomorrow morning. Give Mother the best place, my brother right beside her, me a little to the side — only not too far away! And the little one at my right breast. No one else will lie beside me! — To nestle close to your side, that was a sweet, lovely happiness! But now it won't work for me anymore. It's as if I had to force myself to come to you, as if you were thrusting me away. And yet it's you, and you look so kind, so pious.
FAUST. If you feel it's me, then come!
MARGARET. Out there?
FAUST. Into freedom.
MARGARET. If the grave is out there, if death lurks — then come! From here into the eternal bed of rest, and not a step further. — Are you going now? O Heinrich, if I could go with you!
FAUST. You can! Just will it! The door stands open.

MARGARET. I dare not go out; for me there is nothing to hope. What good is it to flee? They lie in wait for me anyway. It is so wretched to have to beg, and to do it with a bad conscience besides! It is so wretched to wander in foreign parts, and they will catch me anyway!
FAUST. I'll stay with you.

MARGARET. Quick! Quick! Save your poor child. Off! Always the path along the brook, up over the bridge, into the forest, to the left where the plank stands, in the pond. Catch hold of it at once! It's trying to lift itself, it's still struggling! Save! Save!
FAUST. Pull yourself together! Just one step, and you are free!

MARGARET. If only we were past the mountain! There sits my mother on a stone — it grasps me cold by the hair! There sits my mother on a stone, and her head wags. She does not beckon, she does not nod, her head is heavy on her; she slept so long, she'll wake no more. She slept so that we might enjoy ourselves. They were happy times!
FAUST. If no pleading helps, no telling helps — then I'll dare to carry you off!
MARGARET. Let me be! No, I'll suffer no force! Don't seize me so murderously! I did everything for you out of love.
FAUST. The day is breaking! Sweetheart! Sweetheart!

MARGARET. Day! Yes, day comes! The last day breaks in! It was supposed to be my wedding-day! Tell no one that you've already been with Gretchen. Woe to my wreath! It's already happened! We shall meet again — but not at the dance. The crowd presses; you cannot hear them. The square, the streets cannot hold them. The bell calls, the little staff is broken. How they bind me and seize me! I'm already swept off to the block. Already at every neck the blade twitches that twitches at mine. The world lies mute as the grave!
FAUST. Oh, that I had never been born!
MEPHISTOPHELES [appearing outside]. Up! or you are lost. Useless wavering! Hesitating and prattling! My horses shudder; the morning is dawning.
MARGARET. What is rising up from the ground? Him! Him! Send him away! What does he want at this holy place? He wants me!
FAUST. You shall live!
MARGARET. Judgment of God! To you I have given myself!
MEPHISTOPHELES [to FAUST]. Come! Come! I'll abandon you with her.
MARGARET. I am yours, Father! Save me! You angels! You holy hosts, encamp around me to protect me! Heinrich! I shudder at you.
MEPHISTOPHELES. She is judged!
VOICE FROM ABOVE. Is saved!
MEPHISTOPHELES [to FAUST]. Here to me!
[Vanishes with FAUST.]
VOICE FROM WITHIN, dying away. Heinrich! Heinrich!
